questions.q: Going from A to B along the top path you meet a 6 V rise then a 2 V drop. The bottom path has one element. By KVL, how many volts does the bottom element change the potential from A to B? (rise positive)
questions.w: The potential difference between two points is the same along every path.
sol: Top path: +6 − 2 = +4 V.
The bottom path must also give +4 V.
So the bottom element is a 4 V rise.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A loop has a 12 V battery and resistors R1 and R2 in series. A student writes 12 − IR1 + IR2 = 0. The error is:
o: IR2 should be a drop (−IR2), since the same current flows through it the same way
KVL should sum to the battery voltage, not zero
questions.w: Both resistors are drops going with the current: 12 − IR1 − IR2 = 0.
sol: Same current direction through both resistors.
Each makes a drop.
A sign flip on one resistor is the classic KVL mistake.
From your notes · Diodes and LEDs (area vii): Series LEDs: same current; drops add; the supply must exceed the sum.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Four wires meet at a junction: A brings in 3 A, B takes out 8 A, C brings in 2 A. Wire D carries current INTO the junction. How many amps?
questions.w: In = out: 3 + 2 + I_D = 8.
sol: Currents in: 3 + 2 + D.
Currents out: 8.
D = 3 A.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A 12 V battery (2 Ω) and a 3 V battery (1 Ω) are joined with OPPOSITE polarity across a shared 3 Ω resistor: the 3 V battery acts as −3 V at the top node. Find the voltage across the 3 Ω resistor in volts.
questions.w: Treat the reversed battery as a −3 V source and write one node equation.
sol: Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries E₁ = 12 V (R₁ = 2 Ω) and E₂ = 6 V (R₂ = 1 Ω) feed a shared 3 Ω resistor. Find the total power dissipated in all three resistors, in watts.
questions.w: Find the three currents, then add I²R, or use power supplied = E₁I₁ + E₂I₂.
sol: Supplied = 12 × 2.73 + 6 × -0.545 = 29.5 W, and I²R adds to 29.5 W.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A network has 5 nodes. How many independent KCL equations can you write?
questions.w: The last node's equation is just the sum of the others, so it adds nothing.
sol: Each node gives one KCL equation.
Add all five: every current appears once as in and once as out, giving 0 = 0.
So only 5 − 1 = 4 are independent.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A single loop has a 9 V source, a 3 Ω resistor and an unknown resistor R. The 3 Ω has 6 V across it. What is R?
questions.w: KVL gives R's drop (3 V), and the loop current comes from the known resistor.
sol: Drop across R = 9 − 6 = 3 V.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Currents of 2.4 A and 0.9 A flow into a node, and 1.5 A flows out on a third wire. The fourth wire carries:
questions.w: Count everything in and everything out, then the leftover decides the direction.
sol: Out so far: 1.5 A.
Still 1.8 A must leave, so wire four carries 1.8 A out.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: What does LED stand for?
questions.w: An LED is a diode that gives off light.
sol: Diode = one-way valve for current.
LED = a one-way valve that glows when current flows the right way.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: The end of a diode marked with a stripe or bar is the:
questions.w: The bar is the cathode, the end current leaves.
sol: Think of the symbol as an arrow pointing into a wall.
The arrow (triangle) is the anode side; the wall (bar) is the cathode.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Why does an LED circuit need a series resistor?
o: Once the LED turns on, only the resistor limits the current
The LED needs extra voltage to start
The resistor makes the LED brighter than its rating
The resistor changes AC into DC
questions.w: A lit LED has almost no resistance of its own, so something else must limit current.
sol: Picture a garden hose with no nozzle: the water just gushes.
The LED drop is nearly fixed, so the leftover voltage lands on the resistor and Ohm's law sets the current.
Without it, current climbs until the LED burns out.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 5.0 V supply feeds a red LED (2.0 V drop) and a resistor in series. What voltage is across the resistor?
questions.w: Series voltages add up to the supply, so the resistor gets what the LED leaves.
sol: Supply = LED drop + resistor drop.
Common slip: forgetting the LED uses up part of the voltage.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 5.0 V source, a silicon diode wired backwards and a 1 kΩ resistor are in series. What is the voltage across the diode, in volts?
questions.w: A reverse-biased diode blocks, so it takes the whole supply.
sol: Reverse bias widens the barrier, like a closed gate.
Almost no current flows, so the resistor has about 0 V (V = IR with I ≈ 0).
All 5 V must therefore appear across the gate: the diode.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A silicon diode is in series with a 5 V source and a 1 kΩ load, forward biased. The voltage across the load is about:
questions.w: The diode takes about 0.7 V first; the load gets what is left.
sol: Think of the diode as a toll booth that always charges 0.7 V.
5.0 − 0.7 = 4.3 V for the load.
Mistake: assuming a conducting diode drops 0 V or the full supply.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A white LED (about 3 V drop) is tried on a 3.0 V coin cell with a resistor in series. Most likely it will:
o: stay dark or glow very faintly
light only when the cell is reversed
questions.w: The drop alone nearly uses the whole supply, so little voltage is left to push current.
sol: Series resistor voltage = 3.0 − 3.0 ≈ 0 V.
Little voltage across the resistor means almost no current.
Picture a hill: the LED's 3 V climb eats all the height, leaving nothing to roll.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): Why AC transmission uses very high voltage: P = VI, so the same power at higher V needs less current, and line loss is I²R.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A microcontroller pin gives 3.3 V. A red LED (2.0 V drop) needs 5 mA. Find the series resistor, in ohms.
questions.w: Leftover voltage divided by the wanted current.
sol: Leftover = 3.3 − 2.0 = 1.3 V.
Convert mA to A first: 5 mA = 0.005 A.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A red LED (2.0 V drop) carries 20 mA from 12 V. Find the power used by the LED itself, in milliwatts.
questions.w: Power = voltage across it × current through it.
sol: P = V × I for any part.
Do not use the supply voltage; only the LED's own drop.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 9.0 V battery runs one LED at 15 mA through a series resistor. How much power does the battery supply, in milliwatts?
questions.w: Source power = source voltage × total current. The resistor and LED share it.
sol: The current is the same everywhere in a series loop.
Trap: counting only the resistor or only the LED; the battery pays for both.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Three red LEDs (1.8 V each) in series with a resistor run at 10 mA from 9.0 V. Find the resistor in ohms.
questions.w: Series drops add; the resistor takes what is left.
sol: LED total = 3 × 1.8 = 5.4 V.
Left over = 9.0 − 5.4 = 3.6 V.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 12 V supply and a red LED (2.0 V drop) with a maximum of 20 mA. What is the smallest safe standard resistor (E12: 330, 390, 470, 560, 680, 820)? Answer in ohms.
questions.w: Calculate, then round UP to the next standard value so current stays under the limit.
sol: 500 is not on the list. 470 is below it, which allows more than 20 mA.
Next one up is 560 Ω.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Using the 560 Ω resistor from a 12 V supply and a 2.0 V LED, what is the actual LED current in milliamps?
questions.w: Rounding the resistor up gives a current a bit below the limit.
sol: Resistor voltage = 12 − 2.0 = 10 V.
= 17.9 mA, safely under 20 mA (slightly dimmer).
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: An LED (2.0 V drop) with a 330 Ω resistor each. Two such branches are wired in parallel from 5.0 V. Find the total supply current in milliamps.
questions.w: Parallel branches each draw their own current; the supply gives the sum.
sol: Two identical branches: 2 × 9.09.
Total = 18.2 mA. Like two taps on one water main: flows add.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 5.0 V supply drives an LED (2.0 V drop) through a resistor. If the supply is raised to 10 V with the same resistor, the current becomes how many times larger? (give a decimal)
questions.w: The LED drop stays about the same, so the resistor voltage grows by more than the supply does.
sol: Before: resistor sees 5 − 2 = 3 V.
After: 10 − 2 = 8 V.
8 ÷ 3 = 2.67×. Doubling the supply does NOT double the current.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 9 V battery rated 500 mAh powers one LED branch drawing 20 mA. About how many hours will it last?
questions.w: Hours = capacity ÷ current. A series loop draws the same current from the battery as through the LED.
sol: Think of mAh as the size of a fuel tank.
The extra volts are burned in the resistor; they do not extend the time.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 9.0 V supply, an LED (2.0 V drop) and a resistor. The LED must still get at least 5 mA to be visible. What is the largest resistor, in ohms?
questions.w: A bigger resistor means less current, so there is a maximum value too.
sol: Resistor voltage = 9.0 − 2.0 = 7.0 V.
Any larger and the LED is too dim.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 12 V battery feeds a 2.0 A motor through a series silicon diode that protects against reversed connection. How much power turns into heat in the diode, in watts?
questions.w: Power = diode drop × current.
sol: The diode always drops about 0.7 V when conducting.
The protection is not free: the diode must be rated for heat and 2 A.
From your notes · Diodes and LEDs (area vii): Diode drops add in series: two silicon diodes = 1.4 V.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Two silicon diodes (0.7 V drop each) are wired in opposite directions in parallel, and this pair is in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5.0 V DC source. Find the current in milliamps.
questions.w: Only one diode can conduct; the other is reverse biased. The pair holds about 0.7 V.
sol: Picture two one-way doors facing opposite ways: current uses the door facing it.
Resistor voltage = 5.0 − 0.7 = 4.3 V.
I = 4.3 ÷ 1000 = 4.3 mA. Drops do not add since only one diode is in the path.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 9.0 V supply, an LED (2.0 V), one silicon diode (0.7 V) and a 470 Ω resistor are all in series. Find the current in milliamps.
questions.w: Add every forward drop, then see what is left for the resistor.
sol: Total drops = 2.0 + 0.7 = 2.7 V.
Resistor voltage = 9.0 − 2.7 = 6.3 V.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 12 V source feeds a 1.0 kΩ series resistor and a 5.1 V Zener diode connected in reverse breakdown. Find the current in milliamps through the Zener.
questions.w: The Zener holds its voltage; the resistor takes the rest.
sol: Resistor voltage = 12 − 5.1 = 6.9 V.
Same series current: 6.9 ÷ 1000 = 6.9 mA.
Zener acts like a pressure-relief valve that clamps at 5.1 V.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: The same 12 V, 1.0 kΩ series resistor and 5.1 V Zener now have a 1.0 kΩ load connected across the Zener. How many milliamps flow through the Zener?
questions.w: The load takes part of the series current; the Zener gets only the remainder.
sol: Total current in the 1 kΩ series resistor = 6.9 mA.
Load current = 5.1 V ÷ 1000 = 5.1 mA.
Zener current = 6.9 − 5.1 = 1.8 mA. The Zener is the overflow drain; if the load takes it all, regulation fails.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 10 V peak AC source feeds a single silicon diode and a load (half-wave rectifier). What is the peak voltage across the load, in volts?
questions.w: The diode only conducts after it wins its 0.7 V toll.
sol: Peak load = 10 − 0.7.
For the rest of the cycle, the diode blocks and the load sees about 0 V.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A bridge rectifier uses four silicon diodes. In each half cycle, current passes through two of them in series with the load. For a 10 V peak AC input, what is the peak load voltage, in volts?
questions.w: Two diode drops (2 × 0.7 V) are lost on the way through.
sol: Path = in through one diode, through the load, back through a second diode.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Why do we always round a calculated LED resistor UP to the next standard value?
o: A larger resistor gives a smaller current, which keeps the LED within its limit
A larger resistor gives more current, so the LED is brighter
Standard values only come in larger sizes
It makes the LED drop voltage higher
questions.w: Current and resistance move in opposite directions.
sol: Think of narrowing a pipe: less flow.
Rounding down widens the pipe, so current goes above the limit.
Rounding up only dims the LED slightly.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A forward-biased silicon diode's voltage changes from 0.65 V to 0.72 V. Which best describes what happens to its current?
o: It rises sharply, many times larger
questions.w: Near the knee, a tiny voltage change causes a huge current change.
sol: The diode is like a steep waterslide after a flat start.
Voltage barely moves (about 0.7 V) while current ranges from mA to amps.
That is why a resistor is needed to set the current, not the voltage.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Two silicon diodes are both forward biased and wired in PARALLEL, then in series with a resistor. The voltage across the pair is about:
questions.w: Parallel parts share the same voltage; their drops do not add.
sol: In series, hills stack (0.7 + 0.7).
In parallel, two paths down the same hill: the hill is still 0.7 V high.
The current splits between them.
From your notes · Diodes and LEDs (area vii): Forward-biased silicon diode conducts with about 0.7 V drop.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A relay coil is on a 12 V supply with a flyback diode across it. Which way must the diode face?
o: Cathode (bar) toward the positive side of the coil
Anode toward the positive side of the coil
In series with the coil, anode to ground
questions.w: In normal operation the diode must block; only the coil's spike makes it conduct.
sol: Normal: positive at the cathode side means reverse bias, so no current.
Switch-off: the coil's collapsing field flips its polarity, so the diode now conducts and loops the energy safely.
Picture a heavy flywheel: it keeps spinning when you stop pushing, so give it a path.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A relay coil is switched off and a voltage spike appears across it. Why?
o: A coil resists sudden changes in current, so it pushes current even after the switch opens
The supply voltage doubles when the switch opens
The relay contacts create static electricity
questions.w: Inductors oppose change in current, like water inertia.
sol: Water in a pipe keeps moving when you slam the valve, causing a pressure spike (water hammer).
The coil's magnetic field collapses and induces a large voltage.
Without a path, that voltage can jump a gap and damage the switch or transistor.

From your notes · Diodes and LEDs (area vii): Uses: rectifier (AC to DC), reverse-polarity protection (series diode, costs 0.7 V), flyback protection across relay coils, Zener (reverse breakdown for a fixed voltage), photodiode and solar cell (light makes current).
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A 5.0 V supply drives an LED (2.0 V drop) with a 150 Ω resistor. Find the current in milliamps.
questions.w: Resistor voltage over resistance.
sol: Resistor voltage = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 V.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A resistor limits an LED (2.0 V) to 25 mA from a 12 V supply. A 1/4 W (0.25 W) resistor is on hand. What is the best choice?
o: The needed 400 Ω resistor dissipates 0.25 W, right at the limit, so use a 1/2 W part
R = 400 Ω dissipates 0.05 W, so 1/4 W is plenty
R = 400 Ω dissipates 0.6 W, so use 1 W
questions.w: Calculate the power, then leave a safety margin.
sol: P = I²R = 0.025² × 400 = 0.25 W, exactly the rating.
Parts running at their limit get very hot, so choose 1/2 W.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A solar cell or photodiode, when lit, can:
o: produce a voltage and push current through a load
only block current like an open switch
store charge like a battery for years
questions.w: Light freeing charges in the junction is the LED process run backwards.
sol: LED: current in, light out.
Photodiode and solar cell: light in, current out.
The junction's built-in barrier sorts the freed charges.

From your notes · Diodes and LEDs (area vii): Uses: rectifier (AC to DC), reverse-polarity protection (series diode, costs 0.7 V), flyback protection across relay coils, Zener (reverse breakdown for a fixed voltage), photodiode and solar cell (light makes current).
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Select ALL true statements about a forward-biased silicon LED or diode.
o: Current flows from anode to cathode
Its drop stays near 0.7 V (silicon diode) once conducting
It behaves like an open switch
questions.w: Forward bias opens the gate: narrow barrier and current flows.
sol: Forward = anode positive.
It is NOT an open switch; that is reverse bias.
The drop is almost fixed, which is why a resistor sets the current.
From your notes · Diodes and LEDs (area vii): Forward-biased silicon diode conducts with about 0.7 V drop.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Match each diode type to its main job.
pairs: Holds a steady voltage in reverse breakdown
Protects against a coil's voltage spike
questions.w: Each diode type uses the junction differently.
sol: Rectifier: one-way valve.
Zener: pressure relief valve.
Flyback: safe loop for a coil's energy.
Photodiode: light sensor.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Order these LEDs by forward voltage drop, smallest first.
questions.w: Shorter wavelength light needs a bigger energy gap, so a larger voltage.
sol: Infrared is low-energy (about 1.2–1.5 V).
Red is about 1.8–2.0 V.
Blue is about 3 V.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: A battery is connected backwards to a series LED and resistor. The LED:
o: stays off, since it is reverse biased
questions.w: Reverse bias blocks the current.
sol: Think of a one-way door pushed the wrong way.
Only a tiny leakage current flows.
Ordinary LEDs can be damaged by large reverse voltage, so check polarity.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: Which circuit part is the best simple choice to stop damage if a battery is connected backwards?
o: a diode in series with the supply
questions.w: A series diode only passes current one way.
sol: Reverse battery: the diode blocks.
Normal battery: it conducts but costs 0.7 V.
Like a turnstile that only spins one way.
Notes|n9|Diodes and LEDs (area vii)

questions.q: What is the SI unit of capacitance?
questions.w: Capacitance is measured in farads, named for Michael Faraday.
sol: 1 farad = 1 coulomb per volt.
Real parts are usually µF, nF or pF because a whole farad is huge.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A capacitor can best be compared to:
o: a small rechargeable bucket for charge
questions.w: It stores charge and releases it later.
sol: Voltage is like the water level in the bucket.
Capacitance is how wide the bucket is: wider means more water per level.
So C = Q/V.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Which capacitor type can be damaged by connecting it backwards?
questions.w: Electrolytic caps have a + and a − side.
sol: The stripe on the can marks the negative lead.
Wrong polarity can heat the part or even make it burst.
Ceramic ones have no polarity.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Convert 4700 nF to microfarads.
sol: Micro is 10⁻⁶; nano is 10⁻⁹.
Divide nF by 1000.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Order these capacitances from smallest to largest.
questions.w: Each prefix is 1000 times the one before.
sol: pico 10⁻¹², nano 10⁻⁹, micro 10⁻⁶, milli 10⁻³.
Each step up multiplies by 1000.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 220 µF capacitor is charged to 5.0 V. Find the charge in millicoulombs.
questions.w: Q = C × V.
sol: Charge = how much water is in the bucket.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A capacitor holds 0.50 mC at 5.0 V. Find its capacitance in microfarads.
questions.w: C = Q ÷ V.
sol: Rearrange Q = CV.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 1000 µF capacitor is charged to 12 V. Find the stored energy in millijoules.
questions.w: E = ½CV².
sol: V² first: 144.
= 72 mJ. Square the voltage, not just double it.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 2.0 mF capacitor is charged to 10 V. Find the stored energy in millijoules.
questions.w: E = ½CV², careful with units.
sol: Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A camera flash capacitor of 100 µF is charged to 300 V. Find the energy in joules.
questions.w: Voltage is squared, so high voltage stores lots of energy.
sol: Even small capacitors can hold a lot at high voltage.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: The voltage across a capacitor is doubled. Which statement is true?
o: The charge doubles and the energy quadruples
The charge quadruples and the energy doubles
questions.w: Q = CV is linear in V; E = ½CV² is quadratic.
sol: Q ∝ V.
E ∝ V².
Mix-up: students swap the two.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: The voltage across a capacitor is cut to one half. The stored energy becomes:
questions.w: Energy goes with voltage squared.
sol: (½)² = ¼.
Halving V halves the water level but the bucket's 'pressure energy' falls fourfold.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Three 10 µF capacitors are in parallel. Find the total capacitance in microfarads.
questions.w: Parallel capacitors add, like adding bucket widths side by side.
sol: Plates in parallel behave like one big plate.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Four 8.0 µF capacitors are connected in series. Find the equivalent in microfarads.
questions.w: Equal capacitors in series: C ÷ n.
sol: C = 2 µF.
Series makes a bigger gap, so less capacitance.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Capacitors of 4.7 µF and 10 µF are in series. Find the equivalent in microfarads.
questions.w: Product over sum works for two in series.
sol: Always smaller than the smaller one (4.7).
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Three 10 µF capacitors are in series. Find the equivalent in microfarads.
questions.w: Add reciprocals.
sol: Pattern: n equal caps in series give C/n.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 10 µF capacitor is in parallel with a series pair of 6.0 µF and 3.0 µF. Find the total in microfarads.
questions.w: Solve the series pair first, then add it in parallel.
sol: Series pair: (6×3)/(6+3) = 2 µF.
Parallel: 10 + 2.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 20 µF capacitor is in series with a parallel pair of 10 µF and 10 µF. Find the total in microfarads.
questions.w: Collapse the parallel pair first, then do the series.
sol: Parallel pair = 20 µF.
Series of 20 and 20 = 10 µF.
Do the innermost group first.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 12 V source is across a 6.0 µF and a 3.0 µF capacitor in series. Find the voltage across the 3.0 µF capacitor, in volts.
questions.w: In series both have the same charge, so the smaller capacitor gets more voltage.
sol: C_eq = 2 µF, so Q = 2 µF × 12 V = 24 µC.
V = Q/C = 24 µC ÷ 3 µF = 8 V.
The 6 µF has 4 V. Small bucket fills to a higher level.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 10 µF and a 22 µF capacitor are in parallel across 5.0 V. Find the total charge in microcoulombs.
questions.w: Parallel caps see the same voltage; add the capacitances, then Q = CV.
sol: C_total = 32 µF.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: What capacitor must be placed in series with a 6.0 µF capacitor to give an equivalent of 2.0 µF? Answer in microfarads.
questions.w: Use 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ and solve.
sol: x = 3 µF.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 10 µF capacitor is charged to 10 V, then disconnected. It is then connected across an uncharged 10 µF capacitor. Find the final voltage across the pair, in volts.
questions.w: Charge is conserved; it spreads over twice the capacitance.
sol: New C = 20 µF, so V = 100 ÷ 20.
= 5 V. Like pouring one bucket of water into two.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Same setup: a 10 µF at 10 V connects to an uncharged 10 µF. What is the total energy after sharing, in microjoules?
questions.w: Energy is lost when charge shares (heat and spark).
sol: Before: ½ × 10 µF × 10² = 500 µJ.
After: ½ × 20 µF × 5² = 250 µJ.
Half the energy is lost, even though charge is conserved.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 100 pF air capacitor has its plate gap doubled. Find the new capacitance in picofarads.
questions.w: C = εA/d, so C is inversely proportional to the gap.
sol: Gap ×2 means C ÷ 2.
Plates farther apart feel each other less.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 50 pF air capacitor has a dielectric with relative permittivity 4 fully inserted. Find the new capacitance in picofarads.
questions.w: A dielectric multiplies C by its relative permittivity.
sol: The material cancels part of the field, letting more charge sit on the plates.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor has its plate area doubled AND its gap doubled. The capacitance:
questions.w: C ∝ A/d.
sol: A×2 and d×2 cancel.
Bigger plates help; bigger gap hurts equally.
From your notes · Capacitance (adjacent): Parallel plates: C grows with plate area and with a dielectric, shrinks as the gap grows.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A capacitor is charged by a battery, then the battery STAYS connected while the plates are pulled apart. The charge on the plates:
questions.w: The battery fixes V; C falls, so Q = CV falls.
sol: V is held by the battery.
Gap up, C down.
Q = CV goes down: charge flows back into the battery.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A capacitor is charged and then DISCONNECTED from the battery. The plates are pulled apart. The voltage across it:
questions.w: Charge has nowhere to go, so Q stays fixed; C drops so V = Q/C rises.
sol: Isolated plates keep their charge.
Gap up, C down.
V = Q/C goes up. You did work pulling opposite charges apart.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 12 V battery, a 1.0 kΩ and a 2.0 kΩ resistor in series, with a capacitor across the 2.0 kΩ resistor. After a long time, find the capacitor voltage in volts.
questions.w: Fully charged, the capacitor carries no current, so the resistors act as an ordinary divider.
sol: Steady state: capacitor = open circuit.
The capacitor just matches the voltage across its neighbor.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 100 µF capacitor. Find the time constant τ = RC, in seconds.
questions.w: τ is the time to charge about 63% of the way.
sol: τ = 1 s.
After about 5τ it is essentially full.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: After one time constant (τ = RC), a capacitor charging from 0 V toward 12 V has reached about 63% of the final voltage. Find that voltage in volts.
questions.w: Charging slows down as the capacitor fills, like filling a bucket whose flow slows when it is nearly full.
sol: It does not fill linearly; each τ closes about 63% of the remaining gap.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: A 16 V-rated capacitor is used on a 12 V circuit that sometimes spikes to 20 V. The best change is:
o: use a capacitor rated above the highest voltage, such as 25 V
use a capacitor with a lower rating
use the same part, spikes do not matter
questions.w: Voltage rating is the maximum safe voltage, like a bucket's wall height.
sol: Above the rating the dielectric breaks down.
Spikes count, so pick above 20 V.
25 V is the next common size.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Select ALL changes that increase the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor.
questions.w: C = εA/d.
sol: Area and ε on top increase C.
Gap d on the bottom: smaller d increases C.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Match each quantity to its unit.
questions.w: Know each quantity and its unit.
sol: C = Q/V gives F = C/V.
E in J.
Notes|n13|Capacitance (adjacent)

questions.q: Where is a bar magnet's field strongest?
o: near the poles, where field lines are closest
questions.w: Crowded field lines mean a strong field.
sol: Picture people in a crowd: dense near the exit.
Lines bunch at the poles.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A magnet's field lines never:
questions.w: Crossing would mean two directions at one point.
sol: A compass at any point points only one way.
So lines cannot cross, like single-lane roads.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A magnet is held still inside a coil. The voltage induced in the coil is:
o: equal to the magnet's strength in volts
questions.w: Only a changing flux induces voltage.
sol: No change, no push.
Like a stopped pendulum: no motion, no effect.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: An ideal transformer has 500 primary turns and a 120 V primary. How many secondary turns give 24 V?
questions.w: Turns ratio equals voltage ratio.
sol: Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A step-up transformer must change 12 V to 120 V. The primary has 50 turns. How many secondary turns?
questions.w: The voltage ratio sets the turns ratio.
sol: Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: An ideal transformer's secondary supplies 60 W to a load. How many watts does its primary take, in watts?
questions.w: Ideal means no losses.
sol: P_in = P_out.
So 60 W.
Real ones lose a little as heat.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A transformer takes 100 W and delivers 90 W. What is its efficiency, in percent?
questions.w: Efficiency = output ÷ input.
sol: The missing 10 W is lost as heat.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: An ideal transformer steps 240 V down to 12 V. The load takes 5.0 A. Find the primary current in amps.
questions.w: Power is conserved, so the high-voltage side has the lower current.
sol: Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A wire 0.30 m long carries 4.0 A at right angles to a 0.50 T field. Find the force in newtons.
questions.w: F = BIL.
sol: Force is at right angles to both.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A 0.50 m wire at right angles to a field carries 2.0 A and feels a force of 0.20 N. Find B in teslas.
questions.w: Rearrange F = BIL.
sol: B = F ÷ (I L).
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force F = BIL. If the current is doubled and the wire length is halved, the force:
questions.w: F depends on the product I × L.
sol: So the force is unchanged.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A transformer's primary is connected to a steady 12 V DC battery. After the first instant, the secondary voltage is:
questions.w: No changing flux, no induction. A transformer is an AC machine.
sol: Steady DC makes constant flux.
Constant flux induces nothing.
The primary may also overheat, since only its small wire resistance limits current.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed toward a coil. By Lenz's law, the coil end facing the magnet becomes:
o: a pole that flips with each turn
questions.w: The induced current opposes the change: it pushes the approaching magnet away.
sol: Pushing away needs like poles: N facing N.
If it attracted, the magnet would speed up and free energy appears, impossible.
Lenz's law is nature resisting change.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Lenz: the induced current opposes the change.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A strong magnet dropped down a copper pipe falls very slowly even though copper is not magnetic. Why?
o: The moving magnet induces currents in the copper that oppose its motion
Copper is attracted to the magnet
Air in the pipe supports it
questions.w: Changing flux induces eddy currents; Lenz's law says they resist the motion.
sol: The magnet's moving field makes swirls of current in the pipe.
Those currents make their own field that pushes back.
Like falling through thick honey.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A compass is placed near a wire. When the current direction is reversed, the needle:
questions.w: The field direction around a wire follows the current direction.
sol: Right-hand rule: thumb with the current.
Flip the thumb, and the fingers' curl flips too.
This is Ørsted's discovery.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Straight wire (right-hand rule): thumb along conventional current, fingers curl the way the field circles.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Two long parallel wires carry current in the SAME direction. They:
questions.w: Same-direction currents attract; opposite-direction currents repel.
sol: Each wire's field acts on the other's current.
Ampère found this.
Remember: parallel currents attract (opposite of like charges!).
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: An electromagnet's current is doubled with the same coil. Its field becomes about:
questions.w: Field grows with the current.
sol: More current means more circling field.
Also more turns would help.
Too much current heats the wire.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Electromagnet A has 50 turns and 1.0 A; electromagnet B has 100 turns and 0.5 A, same size and core. Compare their strengths.
o: About equal, since turns × current is the same
questions.w: Strength follows ampere-turns (turns × current).
sol: Equal.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Electromagnet strength: more turns, more current, soft iron core.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Why does the wire in a homemade electromagnet get warm?
o: Current through the wire's resistance makes heat (P = I²R)
questions.w: Any current in a resistor makes heat.
sol: Thin wire has more resistance.
Keep tests short.
A warm battery and wire are warnings.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A generator coil of 100 turns induces 0.50 V when spun at a certain speed. The same motion with a 300-turn coil gives how many volts?
questions.w: Induced voltage is proportional to the number of turns.
sol: Each turn adds its own small voltage in series.
3 times the turns means 3 times the volts.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A power line has 2.0 Ω resistance and carries 10 kW. At 1000 V, the current is 10 A. How many watts are lost in the line?
questions.w: Line loss is I²R.
sol: That is 2% of the power.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: The same 10 kW is sent through the same line, but the voltage is raised 10 times by a transformer. The line loss becomes:
questions.w: Higher voltage means lower current, and loss goes as the current squared.
sol: I falls by 10.
I² falls by 100.
That is why power lines use high voltage: less lost as heat.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: The job of a commutator in a DC motor is to:
o: reverse the coil current every half turn so the torque keeps the same direction
questions.w: Without reversal, the coil would just stop after a half turn.
sol: The coil is pulled around until it lines up, then the current flips.
This keeps it pushed forward.
Like pedaling: push, push again.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Motor: electrical → mechanical (force on a current in a field, F = BIL; the commutator reverses current each half turn).
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Match each device to what it does.
pairs: Magnet that can be switched off
questions.w: Each uses the link between electricity and magnetism.
sol: Motor and generator are opposites.
Transformer needs AC.
Electromagnet needs current.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Order the steps in a simple generator.
items: The coil moves through the field
The magnetic flux through the coil changes
questions.w: Faraday's law links changing flux to voltage.
sol: Motion leads to changing flux.
Changing flux leads to emf.
emf pushes current in a closed circuit.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Select ALL that a magnet attracts strongly.
questions.w: Iron, nickel, cobalt and steel (iron-based) are ferromagnetic.
sol: Copper and aluminum are not attracted.
Steel is mostly iron.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Why use a soft iron core in an electromagnet rather than hard steel?
o: Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current stops
questions.w: The magnet can then be switched off.
sol: Soft iron magnetizes easily and demagnetizes easily.
Hard steel stays magnetized, like a permanent magnet.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Electromagnet strength: more turns, more current, soft iron core.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A relay is mainly made from:
o: an electromagnet that moves a switch
questions.w: A small coil current switches a larger one.
sol: Coil on: pulls contacts closed.
Coil off: spring releases.
Like a light finger on a big switch.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Which sets how much voltage a magnet moving past a coil induces?
o: How long the wire is not moving
The length of the lead wires only
questions.w: Faraday: emf = turns × rate of change of flux.
sol: Faster motion means a faster change.
More turns add more.
Stronger magnets add more.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: A permanent magnet can be weakened by:
o: strong heating or repeated hard hits
questions.w: Heat and shock jumble the tiny magnetic regions (domains).
sol: Domains are tiny areas all pointing the same way.
Heat or hammering knocks them out of line.
Like a neat marching band scattered.
Notes|n12|Magnetism and induction (adjacent)

questions.q: Which 2-input gate is the exact opposite of OR (output flips for every input row)?
questions.w: NOR is OR followed by an inverter.
sol: OR is 1 for three rows and 0 only for (0,0).
Flip every output: 0 only for three rows, 1 only for (0,0).
That is NOR. NAND flips AND, not OR.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A binary number ends in 1. Is the number odd or even?
o: It depends on the other bits
Only odd if it has an even number of 1s
questions.w: The rightmost bit is worth 1; every other place value is even.
sol: Place values are 1, 2, 4, 8 ... Only the 1 is odd.
So the parity of the number is set by the last bit alone.
Misconception: counting 1s is parity of the bits, not of the number.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 2-input OR gate has one input held at 1. The output is:
o: the inverse of the other input
questions.w: OR with 1 gives 1 whatever the other input is.
sol: OR is 1 if at least one input is 1.
One input is already 1, so the output is locked at 1.
OR with 0 is the one that passes the other input.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: The 2-input gate outputs for inputs (A,B) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) are 1, 1, 1, 0. Which gate is it?
questions.w: NAND is 0 only when both inputs are 1.
sol: List where the output is 0: only (1,1).
AND gives 0 on three rows, so the opposite gate gives 0 on one row.
That is NAND.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: The 2-input gate outputs for (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) are 1, 0, 0, 1. Which gate is it?
questions.w: Output is 1 when the inputs are equal.
sol: The 1s are at (0,0) and (1,1).
Both of those have equal inputs.
That is XNOR (equality). XOR would be 0, 1, 1, 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Even parity: a check bit is added so the total number of 1s is even. The data bits are 1011. What is the check bit?
questions.w: 1011 has three 1s, so a 1 makes four.
sol: Count the 1s in 1011: three.
Three is odd, so add a 1 to reach four (even).
The check bit equals the XOR of the data bits: 1⊕0⊕1⊕1 = 1.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: How many of the 16 rows of a 4-input AND gate output 0?
questions.w: AND is 1 only when all four inputs are 1.
sol: 2⁴ = 16 rows.
Only the row 1111 gives 1.
16 − 1 = 15 rows give 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: How many of the 16 rows of a 4-input XOR (1 when an odd number of inputs are 1) output 1?
questions.w: Odd parity is true for exactly half of the rows.
sol: Choose rows with one 1 (4 rows) or three 1s (4 rows).
Half of 16 is 8: flipping any one input flips the output.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 3-input XOR gives 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1. What is its output for A = 1, B = 1, C = 1?
questions.w: Three 1s is an odd count, so the output is 1.
sol: XOR in steps: 1⊕1 = 0.
Then 0⊕1 = 1.
Odd number of 1s gives 1.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Put the evaluation order for  A + B·C′  from FIRST to LAST.
questions.w: Precedence is NOT, then AND, then OR.
sol: NOT binds tightest.
AND comes before OR, like × before +.
OR is last.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For a 3-input gate, match each gate to how many of its 8 rows output 1.
questions.w: Count rows: AND needs all 1s; OR fails only at 000; XOR is odd parity.
sol: AND is 1 only at 111.
OR is 0 only at 000, so 7 rows are 1.
XOR is 1 when one or three inputs are 1: 3 + 1 = 4 rows.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = (A ⊕ B) + B·C equal to 1?
questions.w: Build the 8-row table in pieces and count the 1s.
sol: List all 8 (A,B,C) rows.
Work out each inner part first, then combine, following NOT before AND before OR.
Count the rows with output 1: 5.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = A′·(B ⊕ C) equal to 1?
questions.w: Build the 8-row table in pieces and count the 1s.
sol: List all 8 (A,B,C) rows.
Work out each inner part first, then combine, following NOT before AND before OR.
Count the rows with output 1: 2.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = NOR(AND(A,B), XOR(A,C)) equal to 1?
questions.w: Build the 8-row table in pieces and count the 1s.
sol: List all 8 (A,B,C) rows.
Work out each inner part first, then combine, following NOT before AND before OR.
Count the rows with output 1: 3.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = NOR( AND(A,B), XOR(A,C) ). Find Y for A = 1, B = 0, C = 1.
questions.w: AND = 0 and XOR = 0, so NOR(0,0) = 1.
sol: XOR(1,1) = 0 (equal inputs).
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = XOR( NAND(A,B), OR(B,C) ). Find Y for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0.
questions.w: NAND = 0, OR = 1, so XOR = 1.
sol: Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = AND( NOR(A,B), XNOR(B,C) ). For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = 1?
questions.w: NOR needs A = 0, B = 0; then XNOR needs C = 0.
sol: NOR(A,B) = 1 only when A = 0 and B = 0.
With B = 0, XNOR(B,C) = 1 only when C = 0.
Only the row 000 works: 1 row.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A′·B + A·B + A′·B′ simplifies to:
questions.w: A′B + AB = B, and B + A′B′ = A′ + B (using X + X′Y = X + Y).
sol: A′B + AB = B(A′ + A) = B.
Now B + A′B′ = B + A′ because B + B′Z = B + Z.
Result: A′ + B. Check A = 1, B = 0: every term is 0, so Y = 0, and A′ + B = 0 too.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: (A + B)·(A + B′) simplifies to:
questions.w: Expand: A + A·B′ + A·B + B·B′ = A + A(B′ + B) + 0 = A.
sol: Multiply out the brackets.
B·B′ = 0 and A·B + A·B′ = A.
So A + A = A. Spot check: A = 0 makes both brackets B and B′, and B·B′ = 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A·B + A′·C + B·C simplifies to:
questions.w: The B·C term is redundant (consensus): when B·C = 1, either A·B or A′·C is already 1.
sol: Look at B·C = 1. Then B = 1 and C = 1.
If A = 1, A·B = 1. If A = 0, A′·C = 1.
So B·C never adds a new 1 and can be removed.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: (A ⊕ B) ⊕ B simplifies to:
questions.w: XOR with B twice cancels: B ⊕ B = 0 and A ⊕ 0 = A.
sol: XOR is associative: A ⊕ (B ⊕ B).
B ⊕ B = 0 (equal inputs).
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: XNOR(A,B) = (A ⊕ B)′ is also equal to:
questions.w: Inverting one XOR input inverts the output.
sol: XOR with 1 inverts the other input.
Inverting one input flips the result: (A ⊕ B′) = (A ⊕ B)′.
Inverting both inputs cancels: A′ ⊕ B′ = A ⊕ B, the opposite.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: By De Morgan, (A·B·C)′ equals:
questions.w: Break the bar, flip the operator, complement each variable.
sol: Break the long bar over the AND.
AND becomes OR.
Each variable gets its own bar.
From your notes · Digital logic and binary (area viii): Break the bar, flip the operator.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: By De Morgan, (A + B′ + C)′ equals:
questions.w: OR becomes AND and every term is complemented, including B′ becoming B.
sol: Break the bar, change + to ·.
Complement each term: A′, (B′)′ = B, C′.
Do not forget B′ flips to B (double negation).
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build a NOR gate?
questions.w: NOR = NOT(OR); OR takes 3 NAND gates and the final inverter is a 4th.
sol: OR from NANDs: 2 inverters + 1 NAND = 3 gates.
NOR is OR inverted.
One more NAND wired as an inverter: 3 + 1 = 4.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build an AND gate?
questions.w: NAND then an inverter (a NAND with tied inputs).
sol: AND = NOT(NAND).
NAND is 1 gate.
Inverter is a second NAND: 2 gates.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the minimum number of 2-input NOR gates needed to build an XNOR gate? (Use the circuit N = NOR(A,B), then NOR(A,N) and NOR(B,N), then NOR of those two.)
questions.w: The four-gate NOR design gives XNOR.
sol: N = A′B′.
NOR(A,N) = A′B and NOR(B,N) = AB′.
NOR of those = (A′B + AB′)′ = XNOR. Four gates.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A circuit is NAND( NAND(A,A), NAND(B,B) ). It behaves as which single gate?
questions.w: The inner NANDs are inverters, so the output is (A′·B′)′ = A + B.
sol: NAND(A,A) = A′ and NAND(B,B) = B′.
Outer: (A′·B′)′.
De Morgan: = A + B, an OR gate.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = NAND( A, NAND(A,B) ). Which expression equals Y?
questions.w: NAND(A,B) = A′ + B′. Then Y = (A·(A′ + B′))′ = (A·B′)′ = A′ + B.
sol: Inner NAND = (AB)′ = A′ + B′.
Y = (A·B′)′ = A′ + B. It is 0 only for A = 1, B = 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 3-input function has Y = 1 for ABC = 001, 011, 101, 111 and Y = 0 otherwise. Y equals:
questions.w: Every 1 row has C = 1, and every row with C = 1 is a 1 row.
sol: Look at the column C in the four 1 rows: always 1.
A and B take all four combinations.
So Y ignores A and B: Y = C.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 3-input function has Y = 1 for ABC = 000, 001, 110, 111 and 0 otherwise. Y equals:
o: A·B + A′·B′ (XNOR of A and B)
questions.w: C does not matter. Y = 1 exactly when A = B.
sol: The 1 rows pair up: 000 and 001 differ only in C.
Same for 110 and 111, so C drops out.
Left: A = B = 0 or A = B = 1, which is XNOR.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = 1 for ABC = 011, 101, 110, 111 (at least two inputs are 1). Which expression matches?
questions.w: Each pair of 1s makes Y = 1: AB, AC or BC.
sol: The rows with two or more 1s each contain a pair (AB, AC or BC).
OR the three pair terms.
A ⊕ B ⊕ C is wrong because it is 0 for 011.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 4:1 mux has S1 = A, S0 = B and data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 = 0, 1, 1, 0. The output is:
questions.w: Output is 1 only for AB = 01 and 10: XOR.
sol: S1S0 = AB picks the input numbered AB in binary.
I1 (AB = 01) and I2 (AB = 10) are 1.
1 when A and B differ: XOR.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 2:1 mux has select = A, I0 = 1 and I1 = B. The output is:
questions.w: A = 0 gives 1; A = 1 passes B.
sol: Select 0 picks I0 = 1.
Select 1 picks I1 = B.
Y = 1 unless A = 1 and B = 0, which is A′ + B.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: To build any 3-input function with an 8:1 mux, connect A, B, C to the select lines. What goes on the 8 data inputs?
o: The 8 output values of the truth table (0 or 1 each)
The inputs A, B and C repeated
Only the rows where the output is 1, one per input
questions.w: Each select combination picks one data input, so that input just holds the output for that row.
sol: 8 select combinations = 8 rows.
Row k is picked by select value k.
Tie input k to 1 or 0 to match the table.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is the Carry-out of a full adder equal to 1?
questions.w: Carry is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1.
sol: Carry means the sum is 2 or 3.
Rows with two 1s: 3. Rows with three 1s: 1.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: How many full adders does an 8-bit ripple-carry adder with a carry input use?
questions.w: One full adder per bit position.
sol: Each bit adds A, B and the carry from the right.
That is a full adder.
8 bits means 8 full adders.
From your notes · Digital logic and binary (area viii): A ripple adder chains full adders.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: In a ripple-carry adder, why does the top sum bit settle later than the bottom one?
o: The carry must pass through each stage in turn
The top bits are larger numbers
The sum bits use a different clock
questions.w: Each stage waits for the carry from the stage to its right.
sol: Stage 0 makes carry c1.
Stage 1 needs c1 before it can make c2, and so on.
The delay adds up along the chain.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the largest number that fits in 8 binary bits? Give the answer in decimal.
sol: 8 bits give 2⁸ = 256 patterns.
They start at 0.
So the largest is 255.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Adding a 0 on the right end of a binary number (for example 101 becomes 1010) does what to its value?
questions.w: Every bit moves one place to the left, so every place value doubles.
sol: Each bit now sits in a place worth twice as much.
Same idea as adding a 0 in decimal multiplies by 10.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Subtract in binary: 10010 − 1011. Give the answer in binary.
sol: Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 4-bit adder adds 1111 + 1111. What 5-bit result comes out?
sol: Each number is 15.
So 11110: carry-out 1 and sum bits 1110.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = A·B + A·C′. A student wants fewer gates. Which factored form equals Y?
questions.w: Factor out A: A·B + A·C′ = A·(B + C′).
sol: Both terms share A.
Distributive law reverses.
Check A = 0: Y = 0 and A(B + C′) = 0. (A + B)(A + C′) would be wrong because it is 1 when B = C′ = 1 and A = 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the contrapositive of P → Q?
questions.w: The contrapositive swaps and negates both parts, and it always has the same truth value as the original.
sol: Converse: Q → P (swap only).
Inverse: ~P → ~Q (negate only).
Contrapositive: swap AND negate = ~Q → ~P.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Statement: "If the switch is closed, the lamp lights." What is its converse?
o: If the lamp lights, the switch is closed.
If the switch is open, the lamp is off.
If the lamp is off, the switch is open.
The switch is closed and the lamp lights.
questions.w: The converse swaps the if-part and the then-part.
sol: Original: if S then L.
Swap the two parts only: if L then S.
The converse is NOT equivalent to the original: a lamp can light for other reasons.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Statement: "If the switch is closed, the lamp lights." What is its inverse?
o: If the switch is open, the lamp does not light.
If the lamp lights, the switch is closed.
If the lamp is off, the switch is open.
The switch is open or the lamp lights.
questions.w: The inverse negates both parts but keeps the order.
sol: Original: if S then L.
Negate both parts, keep the order: if not S then not L.
The inverse is NOT equivalent to the original, but it is the contrapositive of the converse.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Switch logic: switches in series = AND (both closed to light).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which statement is logically equivalent to P → Q?
questions.w: P → Q fails only when P is true and Q is false, and ~P ∨ Q fails in exactly that row.
sol: P → Q is false only for P = T, Q = F.
~P ∨ Q is false only when ~P is F and Q is F, i.e. P = T, Q = F.
The tables match.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which statement is the negation of P → Q?
questions.w: The only way an if-then fails is when the if-part is true and the then-part is false.
sol: Ask when P → Q is false: P true, Q false.
Write that as P ∧ ~Q.
Misconception: the negation of an if-then is NOT another if-then.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: By De Morgan and double negation, ~(P ∧ ~Q) is equivalent to:
questions.w: Flip ∧ to ∨ and negate each part: ~P ∨ ~~Q = ~P ∨ Q.
sol: Break the bar over the AND.
Negate P and negate ~Q.
~~Q = Q, so ~P ∨ Q (which is P → Q).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which pair of statements are logically equivalent to each other?
o: The converse and the inverse of the same if-then
questions.w: Converse is Q → P; inverse is ~P → ~Q. These are contrapositives of each other.
sol: Take the contrapositive of Q → P: ~P → ~Q.
That is exactly the inverse.
So they always match each other, but not the original.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: In how many of the 4 rows of a truth table is (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P) true?
questions.w: That is P ↔ Q: true when P and Q match.
sol: Rows (T,T) and (F,F) have P = Q.
Rows (T,F) and (F,T) break one direction.
2 rows.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: In how many of the 8 rows of a truth table for P, Q, R is (P → Q) → R true?
questions.w: Work out P → Q first, then the outer if-then.
sol: R true: always makes the outer if-then true (4 rows).
R false: need (P → Q) false, i.e. P = T, Q = F (1 row).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: In how many of the 8 rows is P → (Q → R) true?
questions.w: It is false only when P is T, Q is T and R is F.
sol: The outer if-then fails only if P is T and Q → R is F.
Q → R is F only for Q = T, R = F.
1 failing row, so 8 − 1 = 7.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: A statement that is true in every row of its truth table, like P ∨ ~P, is called a ______.
questions.w: A tautology is always true.
sol: Check P true: P ∨ ~P is true.
Check P false: ~P is true, so still true.
Always true means tautology.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Given P → Q is true and Q is true. What can you conclude about P?
o: Nothing; P may be true or false
questions.w: A true Q is consistent with P true or false: affirming the consequent is invalid.
sol: With Q true, P → Q is true whatever P is.
So P can be T or F.
No conclusion follows.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Premises: P → Q and ~P. Which conclusion follows validly?
o: None of the usual conclusions (~Q is not forced)
questions.w: Denying the antecedent proves nothing about Q.
sol: Try P = F, Q = T: both premises true.
Then ~Q is false, so ~Q is not forced.
Q is also not forced (Q = F works).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which is the correct translation of "The relay clicks only if the switch is closed"? (R = relay clicks, S = switch closed)
questions.w: "Only if" points to the necessary condition: the click needs the closed switch.
sol: If the relay clicks, the switch must have been closed.
So R is the "if" part: R → S.
Misconception: "only if" does not mean S → R.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Translate: "The lamp is lit if the switch is closed." (L = lamp lit, S = switch closed)
questions.w: A plain "if" introduces the condition: closed switch is sufficient for a lit lamp.
sol: "X if Y" means Y → X.
Y is the closed switch.
So S → L.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Translate "P and Q are not both true."
questions.w: "Not both" negates the whole AND.
sol: Put the bar over the entire P ∧ Q.
Neither P nor Q would be ~P ∧ ~Q (both false), which is stronger.
~(P ∧ Q) = ~P ∨ ~Q by De Morgan.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let D = battery is dead, S = switch is open, L = lamp is off. "If the battery is dead or the switch is open, then the lamp is off."
questions.w: The "if" part contains the OR group.
sol: The comma after "open" marks the end of the if-part.
The if-part is D ∨ S.
So (D ∨ S) → L.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let D = battery is dead, S = switch is open, L = lamp is off. "The lamp is off only if the battery is dead or the switch is open."
questions.w: "Only if" puts the lamp-off on the if side.
sol: Lamp off needs a cause: D or S.
So L implies D ∨ S.
(D ∨ S) → L is the converse.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let L = lamp is on, S = switch is closed, B = battery is charged. "The lamp is on if and only if the switch is closed and the battery is charged."
questions.w: "If and only if" is ↔; the group S ∧ B sits on the right.
sol: "If and only if" is the double arrow.
Both conditions (S and B) are grouped.
So L ↔ (S ∧ B).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Switch A is in series with a parallel pair of switches B and C. The lamp is on when:
questions.w: The parallel pair works like OR, and the series link with A works like AND.
sol: B and C in parallel: B ∨ C.
That block is in series with A: AND.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Switches A and B in series form one branch. A switch C forms a second branch in parallel with it. The lamp is on when:
questions.w: Each branch is a way for current to flow: either A and B both closed, or C closed.
sol: Branch 1 works if A ∧ B.
Branch 2 works if C.
Parallel branches: OR of the two.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Switch logic: switches in series = AND (both closed to light).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Proof lines: 1. A → B (P)  2. B → C (P)  3. A (P)  4. B (MP 1,3)  5. C (?). The reason for line 5 is:
questions.w: Line 5 uses B → C and B, which is modus ponens.
sol: Need an if-then and its antecedent.
Line 2 is B → C and line 4 gives B.
That is MP. HS would give A → C, not C.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Proof lines: 1. P ∨ Q (P)  2. ~P (P)  3. Q (DS 1,2)  4. Q → R (P)  5. R (?). The reason for line 5 is:
questions.w: Q is true (line 3) and Q → R, so R by modus ponens.
sol: Look for an if-then with a true antecedent.
Line 4 is Q → R and line 3 is Q.
That is MP.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Proof lines: 1. ~A ∨ B (P)  2. A (P)  3. ~~A (DN 2)  4. B (?). The reason for line 4 is:
questions.w: Disjunctive syllogism needs the NEGATION of one side of the OR. The negation of ~A is ~~A (line 3).
sol: Line 1 is ~A ∨ B.
To use DS we must deny ~A, which means having ~~A.
Line 3 does that, so B follows by DS from 1 and 3.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: ~(P ∧ Q), P ∴ ~Q. Is this argument valid?
o: Valid only if Q is false already
questions.w: ~(P ∧ Q) is ~P ∨ ~Q by De Morgan; with P true, ~P is false, so ~Q.
sol: De Morgan: ~P ∨ ~Q.
P is true, so ~P is false.
Disjunctive syllogism leaves ~Q.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: P → Q and ~P → R. Does Q ∨ R follow?
o: Yes; either P or ~P is true, so Q or R
No; the premises share no letter
Only if Q and R are both true
questions.w: Constructive dilemma with P ∨ ~P (a tautology) as the third premise.
sol: P ∨ ~P is always true.
If P, then Q. If ~P, then R.
So Q ∨ R in every case.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Premises: P → (Q → R), P, Q. Which conclusion follows?
questions.w: MP on P gives Q → R; MP again with Q gives R.
sol: P → (Q → R) and P give Q → R (MP).
Q → R and Q give R (MP).
Two modus ponens steps.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: P → Q, R → Q, Q ∴ P ∨ R. Is this valid?
questions.w: Q can be true for a third reason, with P and R both false.
sol: Constructive dilemma needs P ∨ R as a premise, not Q.
Try P = F, R = F, Q = T.
All premises true, conclusion false.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: P → Q and P → R. Which conclusion follows?
questions.w: If P is true, both Q and R must be true.
sol: Assume P.
Then Q by the first premise and R by the second.
So P → (Q ∧ R). The converse does not follow.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let A = 1, B = 1, C = 0 (1 = true, 0 = false). Find the value of ~(A ∧ B) → C. Give 1 or 0.
questions.w: Evaluate the inside parts first, then the connectives in order.
sol: Substitute the values.
Work out each smaller piece.
Combine to get 1.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let A = 1, B = 0, C = 0 (1 = true, 0 = false). Find the value of (A ∨ B) → (A ∧ B). Give 1 or 0.
questions.w: Evaluate the inside parts first, then the connectives in order.
sol: Substitute the values.
Work out each smaller piece.
Combine to get 0.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let A = 0, B = 1, C = 1 (1 = true, 0 = false). Find the value of ~(A → B) ∨ ~C. Give 1 or 0.
questions.w: Evaluate the inside parts first, then the connectives in order.
sol: Substitute the values.
Work out each smaller piece.
Combine to get 0.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Put these proof lines in order to prove R from P → Q, Q → R and P.
questions.w: Chain the conditionals first, then apply modus ponens with P.
sol: Premises first.
HS joins P → Q and Q → R into P → R.
MP with P gives R.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Match each rule to its pattern.
questions.w: Know each short pattern by sight.
sol: Elimination takes a part out of an AND.
Addition builds a bigger AND or OR.
Double negation removes two tildes.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Select ALL argument forms that are VALID.
questions.w: Only modus ponens and modus tollens are valid here.
sol: MP and MT always work.
Affirming the consequent (third) fails when P is false and Q is true.
Denying the antecedent (fourth) fails in the same row.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Select ALL statements equivalent to P → Q.
questions.w: The contrapositive, the OR form and the negated-failure form all match P → Q. The converse and inverse do not.
sol: Each true option is false only in the row P = T, Q = F.
Q → P is false in the row P = F, Q = T.
~P → ~Q (inverse) is also false in that row.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Select ALL statements that are tautologies (always true).
questions.w: Test the last two with P = T, Q = F: both come out false.
sol: The first three can never fail.
P → (P ∧ Q) fails at P = T, Q = F.
(P → Q) → (Q → P) fails at P = F, Q = T (P → Q true, Q → P false).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: One row of the truth table shows that BOTH affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid. It is:
questions.w: With P false and Q true, P → Q is true, ~P is true and Q is true, yet P and ~Q are both false.
sol: Affirming: P → Q, Q ∴ P. Premises true, P false.
Denying: P → Q, ~P ∴ ~Q. Premises true, ~Q false.
Both break in the row P = F, Q = T.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Premises: P ↔ Q and ~P. Which conclusion follows?
questions.w: P ↔ Q includes Q → P; with ~P, modus tollens gives ~Q.
sol: P ↔ Q means (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P).
Use Q → P and ~P.
Modus tollens: ~Q.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: "If the circuit is shorted, the fuse blows. The fuse blew. So the circuit was shorted." This argument is:
questions.w: A fuse can blow for another reason, such as an overload.
sol: Form: S → F, F ∴ S.
That reverses modus ponens.
Another cause of F is enough to break it.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: "If the switch is closed, the lamp lights. The lamp does not light. So the switch is open." This argument is:
questions.w: Closed switch would force a lit lamp, so an unlit lamp means the switch is not closed.
sol: Form: S → L, ~L ∴ ~S.
That is modus tollens.
"Open" means not closed.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Premises: A → B, ~B, A ∨ C. Which conclusion follows?
questions.w: MT with the first two gives ~A; then DS on A ∨ C leaves C.
sol: A → B and ~B give ~A (modus tollens).
A ∨ C and ~A give C (disjunctive syllogism).
Two steps.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Premises: (P ∧ Q) → R, P, Q. To reach R you need these steps in order:
o: Conjunctive addition (P ∧ Q), then modus ponens
questions.w: The antecedent is P ∧ Q, so build it from P and Q first.
sol: MP needs the full antecedent.
Conjunctive addition makes P ∧ Q.
Then MP with (P ∧ Q) → R.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: P ∨ Q and ~P ∨ R. Which conclusion follows?
questions.w: If P is true, ~P is false so R is true; if P is false, Q is true. Either way Q ∨ R.
sol: Case P true: second premise gives R.
Case P false: first premise gives Q.
In both cases Q ∨ R. (This is the resolution rule.)
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: "The lamp is lit only if the switch is closed." Which situation would make this statement FALSE?
questions.w: The statement forbids a lit lamp with an open switch.
sol: Write it as L → S.
False only when L is true and S is false.
Lamp off with a closed switch is allowed.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: A student says: "P ∨ Q and ~P ∴ Q is valid, so P ∨ Q and Q ∴ ~P must be valid too." What is wrong?
o: The OR is inclusive, so Q true does not rule out P
The conclusion should be P, not ~P
Affirming Q removes the need for P
questions.w: DS denies one side to get the other. Affirming one side proves nothing about the other.
sol: Try P = T, Q = T.
Premises P ∨ Q and Q are true.
~P is false, so the argument fails.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

hist: Seven names to know: Coulomb, Volta, Ampère, Ohm, Kirchhoff, Boole, Hertz. Each one gave us a law, a unit, or a tool. Learn one clue per person.
Measured the push and pull between charges. Force gets weaker fast as distance grows. His name is the unit of charge: the coulomb (C).
Stacked zinc and copper discs with wet cloth. This "voltaic pile" was the first battery. His name is the unit of voltage: the volt (V).
Showed that wires carrying current push or pull on each other. He linked electricity and magnetism. His name is the unit of current: the ampere (A).
Found that current depends on voltage and resistance.
Two rules for circuits. Current in = current out at a junction. Voltages around a loop add up to zero.
Built an algebra with only TRUE and FALSE (1 and 0). Every logic gate and computer uses his math.
Proved radio waves are real. His name is the unit of frequency: 1 hertz = 1 cycle per second.
Charge = Coulomb. Voltage = Volta. Current = Ampère. Resistance = Ohm. Frequency = Hertz. Logic = Boole. Loops and junctions = Kirchhoff.
static: Positive and negative. Opposites attract. Likes repel. Think of magnets: the same idea.
In solids, only electrons move. Gain electrons and you are negative. Lose electrons and you are positive.
Charge that stays put. It has voltage but no steady current. Rubbing two insulators (balloon and hair) moves electrons from one to the other.
Dry air lets charge pile up. Humid air lets it leak away. That is why winter shocks are common.
Force between two charges. Bigger charges mean a bigger force. More distance means a much smaller force.
Double the distance and the force drops to 1/4. Triple it and the force drops to 1/9. Use meters and coulombs in the formula.
1 µC = 0.000001 C. 1 nC = 0.000000001 C. 1 cm = 0.01 m. Convert BEFORE you plug in numbers.
The push each charge would feel. It points away from + and toward −. Strength is force per charge.
The balloon pushes like charges away inside the wall and pulls opposite charges close. Closer opposite charges win, so it sticks.
Bring a charged rod near (not touching) a metal ball, ground the ball, remove the ground, then remove the rod. The ball keeps the OPPOSITE charge.
dcac: DC flows one way (batteries, solar, USB). AC flips direction again and again (wall outlets).
DC: batteries, solar cells, rectified chargers. AC: generators and power plants.
Transformers can raise AC voltage cheaply. High voltage means low current, so less heat is lost in the wires.
Connect plus to minus and voltages add. Four 1.5 V cells make 6 V.
Connect plus to plus. Voltage stays the same but the battery lasts longer.
Two different metals in a juicy or salty liquid make a cell. Lemon with copper and steel is about 0.7 V. Potato with copper and zinc is about 1.2 V. More cells in series make more voltage.
Frequency is cycles per second. Period is the time of one cycle.
Wall "120 V" is the RMS value. The peak is higher, about 170 V.
Current through the body does the harm. About 10–20 mA can lock muscles. Wet skin lets more current through. Respect every outlet.
Hot carries the voltage. Neutral carries the return current. Ground is only a safety path if something goes wrong.
virpe: Voltage (V) is the push. Current (I) is the flow. Resistance (R) is the squeeze. Power (P) is how fast energy is used.
Know two, find the third. Cover the one you want in the triangle.
V = I × R   I = V / R   R = V / I
Three versions. Pick the one that uses numbers you already have.
Power times time. Use seconds for joules. Use hours with kilowatts for kWh.
Volts times amp-hours gives watt-hours. Divide by watts to get hours of run time.
Wh = V × Ah   hours = Wh ÷ W
m = ÷1000. k = ×1000. µ = ÷1,000,000. Always convert to volts, amps, ohms before calculating.
Longer wire, more resistance. Thicker wire, less. Double the diameter and resistance drops to 1/4.
Black 0, Brown 1, Red 2, Orange 3, Yellow 4, Green 5, Blue 6, Violet 7, Gray 8, White 9. Bands: digit, digit, zeros, tolerance.
Yellow-violet-red-gold means 4, 7, two zeros: 4700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ, ±5%. Gold = 5%. Silver = 10%.
A resistor can overheat. A 1/4 W, 100 Ω resistor can take at most 50 mA.
Keep as many digits as your least precise number. 12.0 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 3.0 A.
circ: One path only. Same current everywhere. Resistances add. If one part breaks, everything stops.
Many paths. Same voltage on every branch. Currents add. Resistance goes DOWN: the total is smaller than the smallest branch.
Quick formula for exactly two resistors: product over sum.
Same-size resistors in parallel: divide by how many there are. Three 90 Ω in parallel = 30 Ω.
A 0 Ω path in parallel makes the whole group 0 Ω. All the current takes the short. Dangerous.
Shrink the circuit step by step. Combine each parallel group, then each series group, until one resistor is left.
In series, each resistor gets a share of the voltage. Bigger resistor, bigger share.
In parallel, current splits. The smaller resistor takes more.
Series bulbs: biggest R is brightest (P = I²R). Parallel bulbs: smallest R is brightest (P = V²/R). Unscrew one parallel bulb and the rest stay lit.
OPEN: a break, no current, full voltage across the gap. SHORT: tiny resistance, huge current, heat.
Voltmeter goes in PARALLEL (high resistance). Ammeter goes in SERIES (tiny resistance). Never put an ammeter across a battery.
A load gets the most power when its resistance equals the source resistance. Speakers are matched this way.
Power supplied should equal the power used by all resistors. Branch currents should add up. Drops around a loop should add up.
kirch: Current going into a junction equals current going out. Charge cannot pile up.
5 A and 3 A flow in. One wire takes 2 A out. The other must carry 6 A.
Go around any closed loop. The voltage rises and drops add to zero.
A 12 V battery and three resistors. Two drop 3 V and 5 V. The third drops 4 V.
1) Draw and label a current in each branch. 2) Write one KCL. 3) Write KVL for two loops. 4) Solve the two equations.
Going through a resistor WITH the current is a drop. Going through a battery from − to + is a rise. A negative answer just means the arrow was backward.
Total power from the sources should equal total power in the resistors.
ctrl: SPST: simple on/off. SPDT: switches between two paths. DPST: two on/off switches moved together. DPDT: two SPDT switches moved together.
Pole = how many circuits it controls. Throw = how many positions each pole connects to.
A thin wire that melts when current is too high. One use. Replace it AFTER fixing the problem. It goes in series with the load.
Trips when current is too high. Flip it back to reset. Slightly slower than a fuse. Fix the problem first.
Find current, then pick the next size up.
Trips at about 5 mA of imbalance between hot and neutral. That missing current is leaking through something, maybe a person. Protects PEOPLE.
A small current in a coil closes a switch in a different circuit. Lets a tiny signal control big power. A diode across the coil absorbs the spike.
Switches in series = AND (both must be on). Switches in parallel = OR (either one works).
Two SPDT switches and two traveler wires. Flip either switch and the lamp changes. Commons go to power and to the lamp.
For switch problems, redraw the circuit for each switch setting.
diode: A one-way valve for current. It lets current through in one direction and blocks the other way.
Two silicon types joined together. P-type has extra holes. N-type has extra electrons. Where they meet is the junction.
Adding tiny amounts of another atom. Group 13 atoms (boron) make P-type. Group 15 atoms (antimony) make N-type.
A thin zone at the junction with no free charges. It acts like a wall.
Positive on the P side (anode). The wall shrinks, current flows. Silicon needs about 0.7 V. Germanium needs about 0.3 V.
Positive on the N side. The wall grows and almost no current flows. It acts like an open switch.
Built to conduct backward at a set voltage. Holds a voltage steady.
A diode that gives off light. Color depends on the material. Red needs about 1.8 V. Blue needs about 3 V. Long lead = anode (+).
Always add one. Find the volts the resistor must drop, then divide by the current. Round UP to a standard value.
In series: same current, drops add. In parallel: give EACH one its own resistor so they match.
Rectifier (AC to DC), reverse-polarity protection, relay protection, voltage regulator.
logic: Everything is 1 (on, true) or 0 (off, false). A truth table lists every input and its output.
n inputs give 2ⁿ rows. Three inputs = 8 rows.
AND = 1 only if both are 1. OR = 1 if either is 1. NOT flips it.
NAND is AND then flipped. NOR is OR then flipped. They are "universal": any circuit can be built from just one of them.
XOR = 1 when inputs are different. XNOR = 1 when inputs match.
Do NOT first, then AND, then OR. Like multiply before add.
Break the bar, change the sign. Works both ways.
A + A·B = A.  A·(A + B) = A.  A + A′B = A + B.  A·B + A·B′ = A.
Find rows where output is 1. Write an AND term for each row. OR them together. Then simplify.
NOT = 1 NAND (tie inputs). AND = 2. OR = 3. XOR = 4.
Picks one input using select lines. 2ⁿ inputs need n select lines. 8 inputs need 3.
Adds two bits. Sum = A XOR B. Carry = A AND B.
Adds two bits plus a carry. Sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1.
n bits can hold 0 up to 2ⁿ − 1. 6 bits max out at 63.
hands: Short columns of five holes are connected. The long side rails run the full length. The center gap separates the two halves.
Red lead in the V/Ω jack. Black lead in COM. Pick DC volts (straight line). Start on the highest range.
Touch the probes across the part, power ON. This is parallel.
Power OFF. Take the part out, or lift one leg, so other paths do not fool you.
Put a known resistor in series. Measure both voltages. Same current means voltage ratio equals resistance ratio.
Use identical LEDs. Give each its own resistor of the same value. Put the two branches in parallel on the same battery.
Read volts and amps on the label. Power = V × A. Charge time = battery Wh ÷ charger W (divide again by efficiency if given).
Mix series (add) and parallel (shrink) until you hit the target. Check with the meter BEFORE adding power.
Check the obvious first: power on? battery good? switch on? wire loose? Plugged in is the #1 problem of all time.
Draw the circuit and write the voltage you expect at each part. Measure with power on. Compare.
In a series loop, the part with the FULL battery voltage across it is open. Other parts read 0 V. A part reading 0 V when it should have voltage may be shorted.
Eye protection. Low voltage only. Never short a battery. Never use current mode across a source. Every LED gets a resistor.
sym: Short code for if-then thinking. ∧ means AND. ∨ means OR. → means if-then. ~ means NOT.
If P then Q. P is true. So Q is true.
If P then Q. Q is false. So P is false.
P or Q. Not P. So Q.
