Simplification: P∧Q gives P. Addition: P gives P∨Q. Double negation: ~~P = P.
"If P then Q. Q. So P." is WRONG (affirming the consequent). "If P then Q. ~P. So ~Q." is WRONG (denying the antecedent).
mag: Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposites attract. Likes repel. Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets.
They leave north, enter south, and never cross. Closer lines mean a stronger field.
Iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted (ferromagnetic). Copper, aluminum, and gold are not.
A current makes a magnetic field. This was the first link between electricity and magnetism.
Straight wire: thumb along the current, fingers curl with the field. Coil: fingers curl with the current, thumb points to north.
More turns, more current, and an iron core all make it stronger. It turns off when the current stops.
A motor turns electricity into motion. A generator turns motion into electricity. Moving a magnet through a coil makes voltage.
Needs AC. More turns on the secondary means higher voltage.
cap: Two metal plates with an insulator between. It stores energy in an electric field.
How much charge it holds per volt. Unit: farad (F). Most are µF.
Double the voltage and the energy is 4 times bigger.
Parallel: capacitances add. Series: use the reciprocal rule (opposite of resistors).
Once fully charged, it blocks steady current like an open circuit.

glossary: The positive side of a diode. Current enters here.
The negative side of a diode. Current leaves here.
The part doing the work, like a bulb.
A break. No current can flow.
A path with almost no resistance. Huge current.
One path. Parts are in a line.
Many paths. Parts are side by side.
The steady DC value that gives the same heating as the AC.
The voltage direction applied to a diode.
Thin zone at a PN junction with no free charges.
A wire running between two three-way switches.
A gate (NAND or NOR) that can build every other gate.
How far a resistor may be from its labeled value.
Current drawn from + to −. Electrons really move the other way.
stuck: Write down what you KNOW and what you must FIND.
Pick the formula that has those letters. Convert units first.
Plug in, then ask: is the size of my answer sensible?

cards.t: Seven names to know: Coulomb, Volta, Ampère, Ohm, Kirchhoff, Boole, Hertz. Each one gave us a law, a unit, or a tool. Learn one clue per person.

dd.why: Science Olympiad circuit questions love history because each name is a clue. Every one of the seven left a law, a unit, or a tool that you still use. If you tie each person to one thing, you can answer who, what, and when. The order also tells a story: charge first, then batteries, then current and magnetism, then circuit laws, then logic, then radio. Dates are usually asked as which came first.
dd.pic: Draw a horizontal timeline from 1785 to 1887. Mark seven dots: Coulomb 1785, Volta 1800, Ampere 1820s, Ohm 1827, Kirchhoff 1845, Boole 1854, Hertz 1887. Write one word under each: charge, battery, current, resistance, loops, logic, waves.
dd.analogy: A family tree of ideas: each person is a relative who gave the family one thing. The unit name is a family name tag. It stops working because a family tree shows who came from whom, but these seven worked mostly apart.
ways: A timeline with one word per dot.

ex.q: How many years passed between Volta's battery and Ohm's law?

dd.trap: Mixing up who is tied to which quantity. Volta goes with voltage and Ampere goes with current. Make one clue card per person.
dd.tip: Co-Vo-Am-Oh-Ki-Bo-He: oldest to newest.

cards.t: Measured the push and pull between charges. Force gets weaker fast as distance grows. His name is the unit of charge: the coulomb (C).

dd.why: Coulomb used a very sensitive twist balance to measure the tiny force between charged spheres. He found it falls with distance squared. Move twice as far and the force is one fourth. Charge is the quantity that causes this push or pull. The unit of charge, the coulomb, is named for him. Without his measurement, the field and voltage ideas would have no solid base.
dd.pic: Draw two small circles with plus signs and an arrow between them labeled F. Draw them twice as far apart with a shorter arrow, a quarter as long. Add a thin thread holding a bar in a glass jar for the twist balance.
dd.analogy: A flashlight beam spreading out: the farther away, the dimmer the spot. Light is like the force, distance is r. It stops working because light has no pushing between two charges, only the spread idea.
ways: Force between charges drops with the square of distance.
Two 1 uC charges 0.1 m apart: F = 0.899 N. At 0.2 m: F is about 0.225 N.
Force against distance is a curve that drops fast and levels.

ex.q: Two 1 uC charges are 0.1 m apart. What is the force?
steps: Use F = k q1 q2 / r^2.

dd.trap: Thinking the force falls in half when the distance doubles. It falls to a fourth.
dd.tip: Coulomb counts the charge.

cards.t: Stacked zinc and copper discs with wet cloth. This "voltaic pile" was the first battery. His name is the unit of voltage: the volt (V).

dd.why: In 1800 Volta stacked zinc and copper discs separated by cloth soaked in salt water. The chemistry between the metals pushes electrons around. Each pair gave a small voltage, and stacking them in series added the voltages. This was the first steady source of current. Before it, people only had short sparks from static electricity. The unit of voltage, the volt, is named for him.
dd.pic: Draw a tall stack: zinc disc, copper disc, wet cloth, then repeat. Label the top end plus and the bottom end minus. Draw wires from the ends to a lamp.
dd.analogy: A stack of batteries in a flashlight: more cells in the stack, more voltage. Each disc pair is a cell. It stops working because a flashlight uses sealed cells, while Volta's pile dried out and corroded.
ways: A stack of metal pairs in wet cloth makes current.
Each pair about 0.7 V. 4 pairs in series: about 2.8 V.

ex.q: A voltaic pile gives about 0.7 V per zinc-copper pair. How many volts for 10 pairs?

dd.trap: Giving Volta the first generator. He built the first chemical battery.
dd.tip: Volta made the Volt.

cards.t: Showed that wires carrying current push or pull on each other. He linked electricity and magnetism. His name is the unit of current: the ampere (A).

dd.why: Ampere followed Oersted's discovery that a current moves a compass. He showed that two wires with current push or pull each other. Same-direction currents attract. Opposite-direction currents repel. So current makes a magnetic field that acts on other currents. This linked electricity and magnetism into one subject, and the unit of current is named for him.
dd.pic: Draw two parallel vertical wires with arrows pointing up on both. Draw small arrows between them pointing toward each other. Then draw one up and one down with the arrows pointing apart.
dd.analogy: Two lanes of cars heading the same way tend to merge together, while opposite-direction traffic keeps apart. Same direction means attract. It stops working because cars have no field, but wires do.
ways: Parallel currents attract. Opposite currents repel.
1 A is defined by the force between two wires; 3 C in 6 s is 0.5 A.

ex.q: A wire carries 3 C of charge past a point in 6 s. What is the current?

dd.trap: Confusing Oersted and Ampere. Oersted: current moves a compass. Ampere: wires push wires.
dd.tip: Ampere: amps and attract.

cards.t: Found that current depends on voltage and resistance.

dd.why: Ohm found that the current in a wire rises in step with the voltage across it. A bigger resistance gives a smaller current at the same voltage. So current equals voltage divided by resistance. The three quantities are linked in one line. Not every device follows it, but ordinary resistors do.
dd.pic: Draw a graph with V across and I up. Draw a straight line through the origin. Label the slope 1/R. Draw a steeper line for a smaller R and a flatter line for a larger R.
dd.analogy: A hose: pressure is voltage, hose narrowness is resistance, water flow is current. More pressure gives more flow, a narrower hose gives less. It stops working because hoses can be complicated by turbulence.
ways: Volts push, ohms hold back, amps flow.
12 V on 4 ohm: 3 A. On 6 ohm: 2 A.
A straight line through zero with slope 1/R.

ex.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 ohm resistor. Find the current.

dd.trap: Forgetting that Ohm's law only applies to resistors, not diodes or lamps that change as they heat.
dd.tip: Ohm: V = I R, one triangle.

cards.t: Two rules for circuits. Current in = current out at a junction. Voltages around a loop add up to zero.

dd.why: Kirchhoff gave two rules that always hold. At a junction, charge cannot pile up, so current in equals current out. Around a loop, energy cannot be created or lost, so voltage rises equal drops. They hold for any circuit, no matter how complicated. Ohm's law handles one resistor, Kirchhoff handles the whole network.
dd.pic: Draw a junction where three wires meet with arrows in and out and write the sums. Next to it, draw a loop with a battery and two resistors and write the sum of rises and drops.
dd.analogy: Cars at a roundabout: cars in equal cars out (junction), and a hiking loop that returns to the start has zero net height change (loop). Cars are current, height is voltage. It stops working because cars can park, but charge cannot.
ways: Junction in = out. Loop sum = zero.
8 A in, 3 A out, so the other wire carries 5 A. Loop: 12 - 5 - 7 = 0.

ex.q: 8 A flows into a junction. 3 A leaves on one wire. How much leaves on the other?
steps: KCL: current in equals current out.

dd.trap: Using KCL to add voltages. KCL is for currents, KVL is for voltages.
dd.tip: Kirchhoff keeps both books balanced.

cards.t: Built an algebra with only TRUE and FALSE (1 and 0). Every logic gate and computer uses his math.

dd.why: Boole showed that logic can be written as algebra with just two values, true and false, or 1 and 0. AND acts like multiplication, OR acts like addition with a cap at 1, and NOT flips. This lets you write a rule once and check it by calculation. A switch is on or off, so a circuit of switches can follow Boolean rules. All computers are built from such gates.
dd.pic: Draw a small table with columns A, B, A AND B, A OR B. Fill in all four rows of 0 and 1. Beside it, draw two switches in series labeled AND and two in parallel labeled OR.
dd.analogy: A light with two keys: it only turns on if both keys are turned (AND). Keys are inputs, light is the output. It stops working because real keys can be half turned, but Boolean values cannot.
ways: Two values and a few operations: AND, OR, NOT.
A = 1, B = 0: AND = 0, OR = 1, NOT A = 0.
Series switches AND. Parallel switches OR.

ex.q: A = 1 and B = 0. Find A AND B and A OR B.
steps: AND is 1 only if both are 1.

dd.trap: Mixing Boole's algebra with decimal math. 1 + 1 = 1 for OR.
dd.tip: Boole: Binary only.

cards.t: Proved radio waves are real. His name is the unit of frequency: 1 hertz = 1 cycle per second.

dd.why: Maxwell predicted that changing electric and magnetic fields make waves that travel through space. Hertz built a spark gap and a loop of wire to test it, and picked up the signal across the room in 1887. That proved radio waves are real. The unit of frequency, the hertz, means cycles per second. Radio and phones use these waves.
dd.pic: Draw a spark gap with a small loop of wire. Beside it draw a wavy line moving to the right to a second small loop with a tiny spark. Mark the wavy line EM wave.
dd.analogy: Dropping a stone in a pond: ripples spread out and a floating cork bobs far away. Spark is the stone, waves are ripples, loop is the cork. It stops working because water needs a pond but EM waves can travel through empty space.
ways: Hertz proved that EM waves exist.
1 Hz is one cycle per second.

ex.q: A signal repeats every 0.02 s. What is its frequency?
steps: Frequency is the inverse of the period.

dd.trap: Mixing up who proved what. Maxwell predicted EM waves on paper, and Hertz proved them with a real experiment.
dd.tip: Hertz: hurts to say, one hertz per second.

cards.t: Charge = Coulomb. Voltage = Volta. Current = Ampère. Resistance = Ohm. Frequency = Hertz. Logic = Boole. Loops and junctions = Kirchhoff.

dd.why: Each major electrical idea has a person tied to a unit or a rule. A matching trick helps: link the quantity to the name. Charge goes with Coulomb, voltage with Volta, current with Ampere, resistance with Ohm, frequency with Hertz. Logic goes with Boole, and circuit loops and junctions go with Kirchhoff. These are all tested again and again.
dd.pic: Draw two columns. Left: Charge, Voltage, Current, Resistance, Frequency, Logic, Loops. Right: Coulomb, Volta, Ampere, Ohm, Hertz, Boole, Kirchhoff. Draw straight lines matching them.
dd.analogy: Jersey numbers on a team: each player has one number and one position. Quantity is the position, scientist is the player. It stops working because a player can change positions, but a unit name stays.
ways: C goes with Coulomb, V with Volta, A with Ampere, ohm with Ohm, Hz with Hertz.
The unit letter hints at the name.

ex.q: Charge of 2 C flows in 4 s. Name the quantity and the unit that carries a scientist's name.

dd.trap: Matching resistance with Kirchhoff. Resistance is Ohm. Kirchhoff is loops and junctions.
dd.tip: Co-V-A-Oh-H-B-K.

lessons.title: Two kinds of charge · Who moves?

cards.t: Positive and negative. Opposites attract. Likes repel. Think of magnets: the same idea.

dd.why: Matter holds two kinds of charge, called positive and negative. Like charges push apart and opposite charges pull together. The force acts across empty space through the electric field. A field arrow shows the way a positive test charge would be pushed. So field lines point away from a positive charge and toward a negative one. Near a lone negative charge they all point inward.
dd.pic: Draw a small circle with a minus sign. Draw 8 arrows around it pointing toward the center. Next to it draw a circle with a plus and 8 arrows pointing outward.
dd.analogy: Magnets are the same pattern, with poles instead of charges. Charge is pole, and the field is the pull. It stops working because poles always come in pairs, while charges can be alone.
ways: +2 uC and -3 uC, 0.3 m apart: F = 0.60 N, attractive.
Arrows out from plus, in toward minus.

ex.q: A +2 uC charge and a -3 uC charge are 0.3 m apart. Find the force and say if it attracts or repels.
steps: Use F = k q1 q2 / r^2 with sizes only.
About 0.60 N, and attracts because the signs differ.

dd.trap: Putting the sign into F and forgetting what it means. Negative F here only says attract.
dd.tip: Plus out, minus in.

cards.t: In solids, only electrons move. Gain electrons and you are negative. Lose electrons and you are positive.

dd.why: In a solid, the positive nuclei are locked in place. Only electrons, the outer ones, can move. So charging an object always means moving electrons. An object that gains extra electrons is negative. One that loses electrons is positive. When glass is rubbed with silk, electrons leave the glass and go to the silk. The glass becomes positive and the silk becomes negative.
dd.pic: Draw a glass rod and a piece of silk touching. Draw small arrows with minus signs moving from the glass to the silk. Then draw them apart, glass labeled plus and silk labeled minus.
dd.analogy: Passing candy between two kids: the one who gives away candy has less (positive), and the one who gets it has more (negative). Candy is electrons. It stops working because candy has real size, but electrons are tiny.
ways: Only electrons move. Gain is negative, loss is positive.
Remove 1e12 electrons: charge is +1.6e-7 C, or +0.16 uC.

ex.q: A rod loses 1.0 x 10^12 electrons. What is its charge? (e = 1.6e-19 C)
steps: Electrons are negative, so losing them leaves plus.

dd.trap: Saying protons moved. In solids, only electrons move.
dd.tip: Lose a minus, get a plus.

cards.t: Charge that stays put. It has voltage but no steady current. Rubbing two insulators (balloon and hair) moves electrons from one to the other.

dd.why: Static means charge that stays on the object. It sits there because insulators do not let it flow. It has voltage but no steady current. Rubbing two insulators together pulls electrons from one to the other, since their atoms hold electrons with different strength. Then the charges are stuck on their surfaces. They only flow suddenly when a spark finds a path.
dd.pic: Draw a balloon and a patch of hair. Show small minus signs moving from hair to balloon as they rub. Then show the balloon with a cluster of minus signs and the hair with plus signs.
dd.analogy: A water balloon before it pops: pressure built up with no flow. Charge is the water, spark is the pop. It stops working because water is a fluid, but charge sits still on insulators.
ways: Charge stays put. Voltage but no steady current.
5 nC on a balloon is about 3.1e10 electrons.

ex.q: A balloon gains 5.0 nC. How many electrons did it pick up?

dd.trap: Thinking static has current. It has voltage, but no steady flow.
dd.tip: Static stays; current goes.

lessons.title: Dry air, more shocks · Coulomb's Law

cards.t: Dry air lets charge pile up. Humid air lets it leak away. That is why winter shocks are common.

dd.why: Water vapor in humid air lets charge leak away from surfaces. Dry air is a better insulator, so the charge stays and keeps adding up as you walk on a carpet. Then a big voltage builds up. When you touch a metal doorknob, it all moves at once as a shock. That is why winter shocks are common, because heated indoor air is very dry.
dd.pic: Draw a stick figure on a carpet with minus signs gathering on the body. Draw a doorknob with a small spark between them. Draw tiny water drops around the figure in a second sketch and arrows carrying the minus signs away.
dd.analogy: A bucket with a leak: humid air is a leaky bucket and dry air is a sealed bucket. Charge is water. It stops working because a leaky bucket drains downward, while charge can go in any direction.
ways: Dry air keeps charge. Humid air lets it leak.
Suppose humidity halves the charge every 2 s: after 6 s only 12.5% is left.

ex.q: Suppose in humid air the charge halves every 2 s. What fraction is left after 6 s?

dd.trap: Blaming cold temperature. It is the dry air that matters.
dd.tip: Dry air, charge stays there.

cards.t: Force between two charges. Bigger charges mean a bigger force. More distance means a much smaller force.

lab.hook: Move the charges. How does the force change?

pre.q: Double the distance between two charges. The force becomes…
pre.why: Force depends on 1/d². Twice as far = 1/4 the force.

dd.why: Force grows with both charges because each charge adds its own push. Double either one and the force doubles. Force falls with the square of the distance because the influence spreads over a sphere. Twice as far means four times the area, so a quarter of the force. Putting them together gives F = k q1 q2 / r^2.
dd.pic: Draw two circles with arrows between them. Under it draw a second pair with one circle labeled 4q and the distance labeled 3r. Write the ratio of forces under the pair.
dd.analogy: The brightness of a lamp: a brighter bulb (more charge) means more light, but the farther away you stand, the dimmer it gets by the square. It stops working because a lamp only shines, while charges push each other.
ways: More charge, more force. More distance, much less.
q1 x4 and r x3: factor 4 / 9. q x2 and r x5: 2 / 25.
Charges multiply, distance squares and divides.

ex.q: One charge is multiplied by 4 and the distance by 3. What is the new force in terms of F?
steps: Force is proportional to q1 q2 / r^2.
q1 x4 gives a factor 4 on top.
r x3 gives 3^2 = 9 on the bottom.

dd.trap: Using r instead of r^2. Always square the distance.
dd.tip: Top times, bottom squares.

cards.t: Double the distance and the force drops to 1/4. Triple it and the force drops to 1/9. Use meters and coulombs in the formula.

dd.why: The inverse-square law is about geometry. Force spreads out like light over the surface of a sphere, and a sphere's area grows with r^2. Double the distance and the force drops to a quarter. Triple it and it drops to a ninth. This is why even a small step away changes the force a lot. Use meters and coulombs, or the constant k will not fit.
dd.pic: Draw a point charge in the middle. Draw one circle at distance r and another at distance 2r. Show the larger circle has four boxes of area for every one box of the smaller circle.
dd.analogy: A sound from a speaker: halve the distance and it gets much louder. Sound spreads like force. It stops working because sound needs air, while the electric force works in a vacuum.
ways: Double distance, a quarter of the force.
r = 1, 2, 3: force = 1, 1/4, 1/9. Half the distance: 4 times.
A steep curve dropping then flattening.

ex.q: One charge is multiplied by 3 and the distance by 2. What is the new force?
steps: Charge x3 puts a factor 3 on top.
Distance x2 gives 2^2 = 4 on the bottom.

dd.trap: Dividing distance by 2 instead of by 4 when it is doubled.
dd.tip: Double the gap, quarter the zap.

cards.t: 1 µC = 0.000001 C. 1 nC = 0.000000001 C. 1 cm = 0.01 m. Convert BEFORE you plug in numbers.

dd.why: Coulomb's law only works in base units: coulombs and meters. Micro means millionth, nano means billionth, and centi means hundredth. If you plug in 3 for 3 uC, the answer is a million times too big. So convert first. Write the number in scientific notation to keep track. Always check that your answer is a sensible size.
dd.pic: Draw a small ladder with rungs labeled C, mC, uC, nC. Beside each, write the power of ten: 1, 10^-3, 10^-6, 10^-9. Add a rung for m, cm, mm.
dd.analogy: Dollars and cents: 3 cents is 0.03 dollars. You have to convert before adding with dollars. Micro is like a tiny cent. It stops working because cents are only hundredths, but micro is millionths.
ways: Convert to C and m first.

ex.q: Find the force between 3 uC and 5 uC charges 2 cm apart.
steps: Convert: 3 uC = 3e-6 C and 5 uC = 5e-6 C.

dd.trap: Plugging in the micro numbers directly.
dd.tip: Convert before you plug.

cards.t: The push each charge would feel. It points away from + and toward −. Strength is force per charge.

dd.why: An electric field is a way to describe the push at a point without needing the second charge. It is the force each unit of charge would feel. So you divide force by the test charge. Doubling the test charge doubles the force, but the ratio stays the same. That means the field belongs to the place and the source, not the test charge. By convention it points the way a positive charge would be pushed.
dd.pic: Draw a big plus charge in the middle. At a point to the right, draw a small test charge and an arrow showing the force. Write E = F / q with an arrow pointing away from the plus.
dd.analogy: Wind: the wind speed at a spot does not depend on the flag you hang there. The flag feels a force. Wind is the field, flag is the test charge. It stops working because wind is air moving, while a field exists in a vacuum.

ex.q: A 3.0 uC test charge feels 0.12 N. Find E.

dd.trap: Using the source charge instead of the test charge in E = F / q.
dd.tip: Field is force per charge.

cards.t: The balloon pushes like charges away inside the wall and pulls opposite charges close. Closer opposite charges win, so it sticks.

dd.why: A neutral wall has equal plus and minus charge. A negative balloon pushes the wall's electrons slightly away and leaves plus charge near the surface. The wall's atoms do not lose charge, they just shift a little. The closer opposite charge is pulled harder than the farther like charge is pushed, because force falls with distance squared. So the pull wins, and the balloon sticks. This is called polarization.
dd.pic: Draw a balloon with minus signs on its right side. Draw the wall with its plus signs shifted toward the balloon and minus signs shifted away. Draw a short thick arrow for the pull and a longer thin one for the push.
dd.analogy: A magnet pulling a paper clip: the clip is neutral but gets a pole near the magnet. It stops working because a magnet needs a magnetic material, while any insulator can be polarized.
ways: Opposite charge at 1 cm pulls 4 times harder than like charge at 2 cm.

ex.q: The near charge is at 1 cm and the far charge at 2 cm. Compare the forces.
steps: The pull is 4 times stronger, so the balloon sticks.

dd.trap: Saying the wall gets charged. Its net charge is still zero.
dd.tip: Near pull beats far push.

cards.t: Bring a charged rod near (not touching) a metal ball, ground the ball, remove the ground, then remove the rod. The ball keeps the OPPOSITE charge.

dd.why: Induction charges a metal ball without touching it. A charged rod brought near pulls or pushes the ball's free electrons to one side. Grounding opens a path to Earth, so electrons can flow between the ball and Earth. A positive rod pulls extra electrons in from the ground. Then you remove the ground first, which traps them. Removing the rod last lets the extra electrons spread evenly. So the ball ends with the OPPOSITE sign of the rod. Order matters: ground off first, rod away second.
dd.pic: Draw a neutral ball with a plus rod on the left. Show minus signs gathering on the left and plus on the right. Draw a wire from the right to ground. Then remove the wire, then the rod, and draw the ball with evenly spread minus signs.
dd.analogy: A seesaw: pushing down one end lifts the other. The rod moves the charges, and the ground lets some in or out. It stops working because a seesaw only moves, while charge actually enters or leaves.
ways: Rod near, ground, remove ground, remove rod. Opposite charge.
The ball gains 3e-9 C: about 1.9e10 electrons.

ex.q: A grounded ball near a positive rod ends with a net charge of -3.0 nC. How many electrons entered?
steps: Positive rod pulls electrons in from ground.

dd.trap: Removing the rod before the ground. The charge would just flow back.
dd.tip: Ground off, then rod off.

lessons.title: DC vs AC · Where each comes from

cards.t: DC flows one way (batteries, solar, USB). AC flips direction again and again (wall outlets).

dd.why: DC means direct current: charge flows in one direction all the time. A battery has a fixed plus and minus, so it pushes one way. AC means alternating current: the push reverses again and again, so charge slides back and forth. The wall outlet in the US reverses 60 times each second (60 Hz). Lamps and heaters work with either, but many electronics need DC and use a charger to convert.
dd.pic: Draw a graph with time across and voltage up. For DC draw a flat horizontal line above zero. For AC draw a smooth wave that goes above and below the zero line. Mark one full wave as one cycle.
dd.analogy: DC is like a river that always flows downhill one way. AC is like ocean waves that push in and pull out at the shore. River = DC, waves = AC. It stops working because a wave moves water forward as well, but AC charge just wiggles back and forth in place.
ways: DC: one direction. AC: reverses direction again and again.
60 Hz AC makes 60 cycles per second. Each cycle has two reversals, so 120 direction changes per second.
DC is a flat line. AC is a wave crossing zero.

ex.q: US wall power is 60 Hz. How many times per second does the current change direction?
steps: 60 Hz means 60 full cycles each second.
One cycle goes forward, then backward.
So each cycle has 2 direction changes.

dd.trap: Thinking AC electrons travel all the way around the circuit. They mostly wiggle back and forth in place. Also, a battery is DC; do not say batteries make AC.
dd.tip: DC = Direct, one way. AC = Alternates, back and forth.

cards.t: DC: batteries, solar cells, rectified chargers. AC: generators and power plants.

dd.why: The source decides the type. A battery or solar cell makes a steady voltage from a chemical or light effect, so it gives DC. A generator spins a coil in a magnetic field. As the coil turns, the field through it rises and falls and flips, so the voltage flips too, which gives AC. Power plants use big generators, so the grid carries AC. Chargers use diodes to turn that AC back into DC (rectifying) for phones and laptops.
dd.pic: Draw a coil spinning between a north pole and a south pole, with a meter next to it. Beside it draw the wave the meter would show. Next to that draw a battery and a flat line.
dd.analogy: A battery is like a water tower, always pushing one way. A generator is like a pedal on a bike: pushes in turns as the leg goes around. Tower = DC, pedal = AC. It stops working because a pedal has two legs pushing, but a generator coil makes the wave smoothly.
ways: Batteries and solar: DC. Generators and the grid: AC. Chargers rectify AC to DC.
12 solar cells at 0.5 V each in series make 6 V DC.
Chemical or light: DC. Spinning coil: AC.

ex.q: Twelve solar cells of 0.5 V each are connected in series. What is the voltage and is it AC or DC?
steps: Solar cells make a steady voltage from light.
A steady, one-direction voltage is DC.

dd.trap: Saying that anything plugged into the wall is AC at the device. Many chargers convert it to DC inside. The wall is AC, but your phone runs on DC.
dd.tip: Batteries stay put, generators go around.

cards.t: Transformers can raise AC voltage cheaply. High voltage means low current, so less heat is lost in the wires.

dd.why: Power plants are often far from towns, so the wires are long and have some resistance. Heat lost in a wire is I^2 x R. Power delivered is V x I. For the same power, raising the voltage lowers the current. Cut the current to one tenth and the loss drops to one hundredth because of the square. Transformers raise and lower AC voltage easily, which is why the grid uses AC.
dd.pic: Draw a power plant on the left, a long thin wire in the middle, and a town on the right. Put a step-up transformer after the plant and a step-down transformer before the town. Mark the wire as high voltage, low current.
dd.analogy: Pushing a crowd through a hallway. One way is to send a few people very fast; the other is to send many people slowly. Fewer people means less bumping into walls. Bumping = heat loss, current = number of people. It stops working because people do not make heat by the square of their number.
ways: Higher voltage, lower current, less heat in the wires.
100 kW through 2 ohm wires. At 1000 V: 100 A, loss 20,000 W. At 10,000 V: 10 A, loss 200 W. 100 times less.
10 times the voltage means 1/100 of the loss.

ex.q: 100 kW is sent through wires of 2 ohm total. Compare the loss at 1000 V and at 10,000 V.
steps: Current is I = P / V, since P = V x I.
Answer: 20,000 W vs 200 W, 100 times less loss at 10,000 V.

dd.trap: Saying that high voltage itself wastes less because it is 'stronger'. The savings come from lower current, because loss is I^2 R.
dd.tip: Volts up, amps down, heat down.

lessons.title: Cells in series · Cells in parallel

cards.t: Connect plus to minus and voltages add. Four 1.5 V cells make 6 V.

dd.why: Each cell lifts charge by a fixed amount of voltage, like one step up a staircase. When you connect plus to minus, the charge climbs one step in the first cell and then another step in the next. The climbs add, so the voltages add. The same current flows through all the cells, so the battery's capacity stays the same as one cell. Four 1.5 V cells make 6 V. If you connect a cell backward, its step goes down and subtracts.
dd.pic: Draw cells as short and long lines (long = plus). Draw them in a row with plus of one touching minus of the next. Under each, write 1.5 V, then draw a bracket under all four with 6 V.
dd.analogy: Climbing stairs: each cell is a step 1.5 V tall, and stacking steps makes a higher staircase. Step = cell, height = voltage. It stops working because a staircase does not get tired, while the cell's capacity (current x time) does not rise in series.
ways: Series: plus to minus, voltages add, capacity does not.

ex.q: Four 1.5 V cells are in series, plus to minus. The last one is accidentally flipped. What is the total voltage?
steps: Three cells are correct: 3 x 1.5 = 4.5 V.
The flipped cell subtracts instead of adds.

dd.trap: Thinking that series adds capacity too. Voltage adds, but mAh stays the same as one cell. Also watch the orientation: a backward cell subtracts.
dd.tip: Series stacks the volts, like stairs.

cards.t: Connect plus to plus. Voltage stays the same but the battery lasts longer.

dd.why: In parallel, plus joins plus and minus joins minus, so every cell sees the same voltage. Each cell can supply its own current, so the total available current and capacity add. That means the battery can run longer or push more current at the same voltage. Cells in parallel should be identical in voltage. If not, the stronger cell pushes current into the weaker one, which wastes energy.
dd.pic: Draw two cells side by side with plus wires connected along the top and minus wires along the bottom. Write 1.5 V next to the pair. Write 2000 mAh on each and 4000 mAh for the pair.
dd.analogy: Two water tanks feeding one pipe. The pressure is the same, but twice as much water is stored. Tanks = cells, pressure = voltage, water = capacity. It stops working because tanks of different heights would act like cells of different voltage, and that wastes energy.
ways: Two 1.5 V, 2000 mAh cells in parallel: 1.5 V, 4000 mAh. At 500 mA that lasts 4000 / 500 = 8 hours.
Parallel gives more time, not more volts.

ex.q: Three 1.5 V, 2500 mAh cells are in parallel and power a 500 mA load. How long do they last?
steps: The units: mAh divided by mA gives hours.

dd.trap: Adding the voltages in parallel. Voltage stays the same. What increases is the capacity and the amount of current available.
dd.tip: Parallel = parked side by side, longer ride.

cards.t: Two different metals in a juicy or salty liquid make a cell. Lemon with copper and steel is about 0.7 V. Potato with copper and zinc is about 1.2 V. More cells in series make more voltage.

dd.why: A cell needs two different metals in a liquid that has ions. One metal gives up electrons more easily than the other, so electrons collect on it. If you connect the two metals with a wire, those electrons flow through the wire to the other metal. The juice or salty water lets ions move inside so the charge can balance. The voltage depends on the metals, so copper with zinc gives more than copper with steel. A lemon cell is weak, about 0.7 V, so you need several in series.
dd.pic: Draw a lemon with two strips stuck in it, one copper and one steel or zinc, with a wire leading to a small meter. Label the strip that gives up electrons as minus. Draw an arrow from it through the wire to the other strip.
dd.analogy: Two kids on a seesaw of different weights: they do not balance, so one side goes down. Metals = kids, tendency to give electrons = weight. It stops working because a seesaw ends up balanced, but a cell keeps pushing until the chemicals are used up.
ways: Two different metals plus an ion-rich liquid make a cell.
Lemon 0.7 V each. Three lemons in series: 2.1 V, enough to light a red LED (about 1.8 V).
Different metals, juicy middle, voltage appears.

ex.q: Each lemon cell gives about 0.7 V. How many are needed in series to reach at least 2.0 V?
steps: Need N x 0.7 to be at least 2.0.
Round up to the next whole number: 3.

dd.trap: Thinking the lemon itself is the power source. The energy comes from the chemical reaction of the metals. The lemon only supplies the acid liquid for ions to move.
dd.tip: Two metals plus a wet middle make a cell.

cards.t: Frequency is cycles per second. Period is the time of one cycle.

lab.hook: AC swings; frequency counts swings per second.

dd.why: Period is the time for one full cycle of a repeating signal. Frequency is how many cycles fit in one second. They are opposites: a signal that repeats quickly has a short period, so T = 1 / f and f = 1 / T. A cycle that takes 0.1 s means 10 cycles fit in a second. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), and one hertz is one cycle per second.
dd.pic: Draw a wave on a time axis. Mark where it begins to repeat and draw a double arrow across one cycle; label it T. Then count the number of cycles in a one second window and write f.
dd.analogy: A swing: the time for one back-and-forth is the period. The number of swings each minute is the frequency. Longer time for each swing means fewer swings. It stops working because a swing slows down, but a clean AC signal keeps the same frequency.
ways: Frequency = cycles per second. Period = seconds per cycle.

ex.q: A signal is 60 Hz. What is its period in milliseconds?

dd.trap: Forgetting the unit change. 0.1 s is 100 ms, not 0.1 ms. Always multiply seconds by 1000 to get milliseconds.
dd.tip: Frequency and period are flip partners.

cards.t: Wall "120 V" is the RMS value. The peak is higher, about 170 V.

dd.why: An AC voltage swings up and down, so its value is not constant. To compare it to DC, we ask: what DC voltage would make the same heat in a resistor? That is the RMS value (root mean square). For a smooth sine wave, the RMS is the peak divided by the square root of 2, about 0.707 of the peak. So the 120 V from a wall outlet is RMS, and the wave actually reaches about 170 V at the top.
dd.pic: Draw a sine wave with a horizontal dashed line at the top peak and another dashed line lower at about 70 percent of the peak. Label the top Vpeak and the lower line Vrms. Show that the wave spends only part of its time near the peak.
dd.analogy: A roller coaster: the highest point is the peak, but the average height of the ride is lower. The RMS is like an effective height. Peak = top of the hill, RMS = the useful level. It stops working because averages can cancel, but RMS is always positive.
ways: RMS is the DC-equivalent value. Peak = RMS x 1.414.
120 V RMS gives a peak of 169.7 V (about 170 V). 230 V RMS gives about 325 V peak.

ex.q: A European outlet is 230 V RMS. Find its peak voltage.
steps: The peak is higher than RMS for a sine wave.

dd.trap: Dividing when you should multiply. To go from peak to RMS you divide by 1.414. To go from RMS to peak you multiply. The peak must come out larger.
dd.tip: Peak is the proud tall one: RMS times 1.41.

cards.t: Current through the body does the harm. About 10–20 mA can lock muscles. Wet skin lets more current through. Respect every outlet.

dd.why: Harm comes from the current through the body, not directly from the voltage. By Ohm's law, I = V / R, so more voltage or less body resistance means more current. Wet skin has much lower resistance than dry skin, so the same outlet can push much more current. Around 10 to 20 mA can make muscles lock so you cannot let go. Larger currents can disturb the heartbeat. That is why you treat every outlet with respect.
dd.pic: Draw a stick figure touching a wire, with a path through the body to the ground. Label the current I, the body resistance R, and the voltage V. Draw two figures: one with dry hands (large R) and one with wet hands (small R).
dd.analogy: Water pressure through a hose: the pressure (voltage) matters, but the flow (current) is what knocks you over. A wider hose (wet skin, low resistance) lets more flow. Pressure = voltage, flow = current. It stops working because hoses do not stop heart muscles.
ways: Current does the harm. Wet skin allows more current.
120 V. Dry skin 100,000 ohm: 1.2 mA. Wet skin 1,000 ohm: 120 mA. (Example values only.)
Low resistance, more current, more danger.

ex.q: Using example values, find the current from 120 V through dry skin (100,000 ohm) and wet skin (1,000 ohm).
steps: Use Ohm's law: I = V / R.
Answer: 1.2 mA dry, 120 mA wet; the wet case is far above the 10-20 mA lock-up level.

dd.trap: Believing only high voltage is dangerous. Even household voltage can be deadly when your skin is wet. These are example resistances; real values vary a lot.
dd.tip: Wet hands, more amps: stay dry and stay safe.

cards.t: Hot carries the voltage. Neutral carries the return current. Ground is only a safety path if something goes wrong.

dd.why: A normal AC outlet has three connections. The hot wire carries the alternating voltage from the panel. The neutral wire gives the current a path back to the panel. Under normal operation the load current goes out on hot and returns on neutral, so those two carry the same size current. The ground wire is a safety path, attached to the metal case, and normally carries nothing. If a hot wire touches the case, the fault current goes down the ground wire and trips the breaker instead of shocking you.
dd.pic: Draw a wall outlet with three slots. Label the short slot hot, the long slot neutral, and the round hole ground. Draw an appliance with a loop: arrow out on hot, arrow back on neutral, and a dotted line to the case on ground.
dd.analogy: A road trip with a safety road. Hot = the road out to the store, neutral = the road back home, ground = the emergency exit used only if something goes wrong. It stops working because exits are used rarely but are always connected.
ways: Hot: out. Neutral: back. Ground: safety only.
A 1200 W hair dryer on 120 V: 10 A on hot, 10 A back on neutral, 0 A on ground.
White = neutral, black = hot, green or bare = ground.

ex.q: A 1200 W hair dryer runs on 120 V. What current is in the hot, neutral and ground wires in normal use?
steps: The same current must return on neutral.
Ground only matters in a fault, so it carries 0 A.
Answer: hot 10 A, neutral 10 A, ground 0 A.

dd.trap: Calling the white wire ground. White is neutral and carries current back. Ground (green or bare) is only for safety. Both go to the panel but they do different jobs.
dd.tip: Hot goes, neutral returns, ground guards.

cards.t: Voltage (V) is the push. Current (I) is the flow. Resistance (R) is the squeeze. Power (P) is how fast energy is used.

dd.why: Four ideas run every circuit. Voltage is the push that makes charge move. Current is how much charge passes each second. Resistance is how hard it is for charge to move. Power is how fast energy is used. Charge is measured in coulombs. Each has a unit: volt, ampere, ohm, watt. If you know the words, the formulas make sense.
dd.pic: Draw a water tank on a platform with a pipe. Label the height V, the water flow I, the narrow part R. Add a small waterwheel and label it P.
dd.analogy: Water flows from a tank through a pipe. Height is pressure (V), flow rate is current (I), narrow pipe is resistance (R), and the wheel turning is power (P). It stops working because water is wet and heavy, but charge is not.
ways: V push, I flow, R squeeze, P work rate.
V in volts, I in amps, R in ohms, P in watts.

ex.q: A 12 V battery drives a 4 ohm resistor. Find current and power.

dd.trap: Mixing up charge (coulomb) and current (ampere). Current is charge per second.
dd.tip: Push, flow, squeeze, speed.

cards.t: Know two, find the third. Cover the one you want in the triangle.
cards.f: V = I × R   I = V / R   R = V / I

lab.hook: Change V and R. Watch I change.

dd.why: Ohm's law ties three numbers together. Push harder and the flow rises. Squeeze more and the flow falls. So current is voltage divided by resistance. Rearranging gives the other two forms. The triangle helps: cover the one you want and read the rest. It works only for resistors that stay steady.
dd.pic: Draw a triangle with V on top and I and R at the bottom. Draw a finger covering V to show I times R. Cover I to show V over R. Cover R to show V over I.
dd.analogy: A school hallway: more students pushing (V), narrower door (R), fewer students per second get through (I). It stops working because people can wait, while charge flows steadily.
ways: V against I is a line with slope R.

ex.q: A 9 V battery drives 3 mA through a resistor. Find R.
steps: We want R, so R = V / I.

dd.trap: Using milliamps directly. Convert to amps first.
dd.tip: Cover and see.

cards.t: Three versions. Pick the one that uses numbers you already have.

lab.note: Both give {=v*i|1} W. R = V/I = {=v/i|1} Ω.

dd.why: Power is the rate of energy use: V x I. Using Ohm's law, you can swap V or I out and get two more forms. I squared R is handy when you know current. V squared over R is handy when you know voltage. All three give the same answer. Pick the one that uses the numbers you have. Efficiency says some input power is lost as heat.
dd.pic: Draw three small boxes: V x I, I^2 R, V^2 / R. Under each draw a mini circuit with the known numbers underlined. Draw an arrow from the one that fits.
dd.analogy: Cooking time: a stove burner can use a big flame (current) or a hot flame (voltage). Both give heat. It stops working because food does not obey Ohm's law.
ways: Three forms of the same power.

ex.q: A 5.0 V charger outputs 2.0 A and is 85% efficient. What input power from the wall?

dd.trap: Multiplying by 0.85 instead of dividing. Input must be larger.
dd.tip: Input is bigger than output.

cards.t: Power times time. Use seconds for joules. Use hours with kilowatts for kWh.

dd.why: Power is energy per second, so energy is power times time. Use seconds with watts to get joules. Joules are small, so electric bills use kilowatt-hours, where power is in kilowatts and time in hours. One kWh is 1000 W for 3600 s, which is 3.6 million joules. The cost is kWh times the price per kWh.
dd.pic: Draw a bar with power on the vertical side and time on the horizontal side. Shade the rectangle. Label the area as energy.
dd.analogy: Driving: speed times time equals distance. Power is speed, time is time, energy is distance. It stops working because distance is only a distance, while energy can change form.
ways: 60 W for 5 h = 0.3 kWh. 100 W for 60 s = 6000 J.
The area of the power-time rectangle.

ex.q: A 1 kW heater runs 3 h at $0.20 per kWh. What does it cost?

dd.trap: Mixing watts with kilowatts in one formula.
dd.tip: kW times hours is kWh.

cards.t: Current times time.

dd.why: Current is charge flowing per second. So the total charge is current times time. A battery rating in mAh is milliamp-hours, which is charge. 1 mAh is 3.6 coulombs because 0.001 A for 3600 s is 3.6 C. A bigger mAh means the battery can supply a current longer. It does not say how much energy it has unless you know the voltage.
dd.pic: Draw a graph with current on the vertical and time on the horizontal. Shade the rectangle under the line. Label the area charge Q.
dd.analogy: Water flowing from a tap: flow rate times time equals the amount of water. Current is flow rate, charge is amount. It stops working because tap water has a mass, while charge is just a count.
ways: mAh is a unit of charge.

ex.q: A device draws 0.5 A for 20 minutes. How much charge flows?

dd.trap: Calling mAh a unit of energy. It is charge.
dd.tip: Amps times time, charge is mine.

cards.t: Volts times amp-hours gives watt-hours. Divide by watts to get hours of run time.
cards.f: Wh = V × Ah   hours = Wh ÷ W

dd.why: A battery's energy is its voltage times its charge, because each coulomb gets that many joules. Volts times amp-hours gives watt-hours. To find the run time, divide the energy by the power draw. Two batteries of the same mAh can store different energy if their voltages differ. Real batteries lose some, so the actual time is a bit less.
dd.pic: Draw a battery with the label 3.7 V and 2 Ah. Draw an arrow to a box that says 7.4 Wh. Draw a second arrow to a lamp labeled 2 W and an hours clock.
dd.analogy: A gas tank: size in liters is charge, the quality of the fuel is voltage, and together they are the energy. It stops working because gas is used up fully, while batteries can lose capacity.
ways: Wh equals V times Ah. Hours equals Wh over W.
3.7 V x 2 Ah = 7.4 Wh. At 2 W: 3.7 h.

ex.q: A 1.5 kW heater runs 4 h at $0.20 per kWh. Cost? Also a 7.4 Wh battery runs a 2 W device. How long?
steps: Heater energy: 1.5 kW x 4 h = 6 kWh.

dd.trap: Forgetting to convert kW and W. Use watts with Wh.
dd.tip: Wh over W gives hours.

cards.t: m = ÷1000. k = ×1000. µ = ÷1,000,000. Always convert to volts, amps, ohms before calculating.

dd.why: Prefixes make big and small numbers short. Milli is a thousandth, kilo is a thousand, micro is a millionth. Formulas assume base units: volts, amps, and ohms. A 250 mA current is 0.25 A. A 4.7 kilohm resistor is 4700 ohm. If you skip converting, answers are off by a thousand or a million. Convert first, then calculate.
dd.pic: Draw a number line with marks: micro, milli, 1, kilo, mega. Write the powers: 10^-6, 10^-3, 1, 10^3, 10^6. Draw arrows showing 250 mA moving to 0.25 A.
dd.analogy: Cents and dollars: 250 cents is 2.50 dollars. You convert to dollars before you use a dollar price. Milli is like cents but per thousand. It stops working because cents are hundredths.
ways: Milli divides by 1000, kilo multiplies by 1000.
250 mA = 0.25 A. 4.7 kilohm = 4700 ohm. 3 mA through 4.7 kilohm: V = 14.1 V.

ex.q: A 3 mA current flows through a 4.7 kilohm resistor. What is the voltage?

dd.trap: Plugging in 3 and 4.7 and getting 14.1 mV or V. Always convert.
dd.tip: Milli small, kilo tall.

cards.t: Longer wire, more resistance. Thicker wire, less. Double the diameter and resistance drops to 1/4.

dd.why: Resistance comes from charges bumping into atoms along the wire. A longer wire has more bumps, so resistance rises with length. A thicker wire gives charges more lanes, so resistance falls with area. Area depends on diameter squared. Double the diameter, area is four times, and resistance falls to a quarter. The material factor rho says how bumpy the metal is.
dd.pic: Draw a long thin pipe and a short wide pipe. Label the long thin one high R and the short wide one low R. Draw dots moving through with arrows.
dd.analogy: A hallway: a long, narrow hallway is slow for a crowd, and a short, wide one is fast. Length is L, width is area A. It stops working because people can push, while charge can only move with the field.
ways: Longer is worse, thicker is better.
10 m of 1 mm^2 copper: R = 0.168 ohm. 20 m: 0.336 ohm.
R goes up with L and down with A.

ex.q: Find R for 10 m of copper wire with area 1.0 mm^2. (rho = 1.68e-8 ohm m)

dd.trap: Using diameter as area. Area scales with diameter squared.
dd.tip: Long is a strain, wide is plain.

cards.t: Black 0, Brown 1, Red 2, Orange 3, Yellow 4, Green 5, Blue 6, Violet 7, Gray 8, White 9. Bands: digit, digit, zeros, tolerance.

dd.why: The bands are a code to read a resistor's value. The first two bands are digits. The third band is the multiplier, how many zeros to add. The fourth is the tolerance, how far the real value may be off. Colors are numbers in order from 0 to 9, the same order as in a rainbow-ish list. Gold is plus or minus 5 percent and silver is 10 percent.
dd.pic: Draw a resistor with four bands. Write digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance above them. Below, write the color list: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9.
dd.analogy: A combination lock: each band is one dial. The first two dials make a number, the third says how many zeros. It stops working because locks have a hidden order, but resistors are read left to right from the end away from gold.

ex.q: Orange, brown, black, gold. Find value and tolerance.

dd.trap: Reading from the gold end. Start from the other side.
dd.tip: Black, Brown, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Violet, Gray, White: 0 to 9.

cards.t: Yellow-violet-red-gold means 4, 7, two zeros: 4700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ, ±5%. Gold = 5%. Silver = 10%.

dd.why: With practice you read colors fast. Yellow is 4, violet is 7, red is 2 (two zeros). So 4, 7 then two zeros gives 4700 ohm, or 4.7 kilohm. Gold means 5 percent. Silver means 10 percent. Check that the answer sits in a sensible range of standard values. Reading in both directions helps.
dd.pic: Draw four bands on a resistor with colors written inside: yellow, violet, red, gold. Draw arrows to numbers 4, 7, 00, 5%. Write 4700 ohm below.
dd.analogy: A phone number: the first digits are the area, the last digit is the extension. Bands are digits in a fixed order. It stops working because phone digits have no multiplier.
ways: Two digits, count zeros, then tolerance.

ex.q: Brown, black, red, silver. Find value and tolerance.

dd.trap: Mixing up gold (5 percent) and silver (10 percent).
dd.tip: Gold is better: 5, silver 10.

cards.t: A resistor can overheat. A 1/4 W, 100 Ω resistor can take at most 50 mA.

dd.why: A resistor turns electric energy into heat. Too much power and it overheats and burns. Each resistor has a power rating, like 1/4 W. The power is I squared R, so the most current it can handle is I = sqrt(P / R). A bigger resistance means a smaller allowed current. Use a bigger rating if you need more power.
dd.pic: Draw a resistor with a thermometer next to it. Draw the limit line at 1/4 W. Draw an arrow from the current to the heat.
dd.analogy: A toaster slot: only so much bread fits before it burns. Rating is slot size. It stops working because a toaster is made to burn bread, while a resistor is not.
ways: Max current is the square root of power over resistance.
1/4 W, 100 ohm: 50 mA. 1/4 W, 1 kilohm: 15.8 mA.

ex.q: A 0.25 A current flows through a 160 ohm resistor. Find the power. Does a 1/4 W rating fit?
steps: A 1/4 W resistor would burn; you need at least 10 W.

dd.trap: Using P = I x R. It must be I squared.
dd.tip: Square the amps, then times ohms.

cards.t: Keep as many digits as your least precise number. 12.0 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 3.0 A.

dd.why: An answer cannot be more precise than your least precise number. Significant figures show that. 12.0 has three, 4.0 has two. A calculator shows more digits but they are not real. So round to the least number of significant figures. This makes the answer honest. In competitions, follow what the question asks.
dd.pic: Write 12.0 / 4.0 on a line. Underline the number of sig figs under each: 3 and 2. Draw an arrow to the answer 3.0 and circle two digits.
dd.analogy: A ruler marked in centimeters: you cannot claim a length to the millimeter. Rounding is the honest measure. It stops working because rulers are physical, and numbers have no gap.
ways: Keep as many digits as your least precise number.
Round to the fewest sig figs.

ex.q: Compute 6.0 V / 0.25 A with the right sig figs.

dd.trap: Writing all the calculator digits. Round to match.
dd.tip: Weakest link sets the digits.

cards.t: One path only. Same current everywhere. Resistances add. If one part breaks, everything stops.

lab.hook: In series, resistors add and the same current goes through all.

dd.why: In a series circuit the wire has no branches, so every charge must pass through every part, one after another. Charge cannot pile up or vanish, so the current is the same at each point. Each resistor adds more squeeze on the same path, so the resistances add up. If one part breaks, the one path is cut and nothing can flow anywhere. That is why old holiday lights went dark all at once when one bulb failed.
dd.pic: Draw a single loop: battery, then three boxes (resistors) in a row, then back to the battery. Write the same arrow and the letter I beside each box. Put a small break in the loop and cross out the arrows to show nothing flows.
dd.analogy: A single-lane road with three toll booths. Every car must go through all three booths, and the traffic rate is the same everywhere. Cars = charge, booths = resistors, cars per minute = current. It stops working because toll booths do not use up cars, while resistors do not use up charge either, but they do use up voltage.
ways: One path. Same current. Resistances add. One break stops all.
100 ohm + 220 ohm + 330 ohm = 650 ohm. On 13 V the current is 13 / 650 = 0.02 A everywhere.
Series: current same, resistance adds, voltage shares.

ex.q: Resistors of 100, 220 and 330 ohms are in series with a 13 V battery. Find the current.
steps: That makes 650 ohms total, because each adds squeeze.
Use I = V / R since the battery sets the total push.
The current is the same in all three resistors.

dd.trap: Students think the current gets used up after each resistor. It does not. Voltage gets used up, current stays the same. Also, a broken part in series stops everything.
dd.tip: Series = single file. One line, one current.

cards.t: Many paths. Same voltage on every branch. Currents add. Resistance goes DOWN: the total is smaller than the smallest branch.

lab.hook: In parallel, current has more paths, so total resistance drops.
lab.note: Total = {=1/(1/r1+1/r2)|2} Ω, smaller than either branch.

pre.q: Two 10 Ω resistors in parallel make a total of…
pre.why: Two equal paths halve the resistance: 5 Ω.

dd.why: In parallel, the battery connects straight across every branch, so every branch gets the full voltage. Each branch pulls its own current, and the currents add up at the junction. Adding another branch gives the charge one more road, so the total current goes up. More current from the same voltage means smaller total resistance. That is why the total is always smaller than the smallest branch.
dd.pic: Draw a ladder lying on its side: a battery on the left and two or three rungs (resistors) between the top and bottom rails. Mark each rung with the same voltage V. Draw arrows splitting at the top and merging at the bottom.
dd.analogy: A store with several checkout lanes open. Each lane can serve customers at the same time, so the total customers per minute rises when you open one more. Lanes = branches, customers per minute = current. It stops working because customers choose lanes freely, but current always favors the lower-resistance branch.
ways: Many paths. Same voltage. Currents add. Total resistance drops.
12 ohm, 6 ohm, 4 ohm in parallel: 1/12 + 2/12 + 3/12 = 6/12, so R = 2 ohm. That is below 4.
Parallel total is always smaller than the smallest branch.

ex.q: Resistors of 12, 6 and 4 ohms are in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
steps: Write with a common bottom of 12: 1/12 + 2/12 + 3/12.
Check: 2 is smaller than the smallest branch (4). Good.

dd.trap: Forgetting to flip at the end. 1/R = 1/2 is not R = 1/2 in this case: the answer is R = 2. Always check that your answer is smaller than the smallest branch.
dd.tip: Parallel = more roads, less squeeze.

cards.t: Quick formula for exactly two resistors: product over sum.

dd.why: The product-over-sum shortcut comes from the reciprocal rule. Start with 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Put the two fractions over a common bottom: (R2 + R1) / (R1 x R2). Flip both sides and you get R = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2). The shortcut only works for exactly two resistors. If one resistor is far bigger than the other, the answer is close to the smaller one, because most current takes the easy path.
dd.pic: Draw two resistors in parallel and label them R1 and R2. Beside it, draw one resistor labeled with the product over the sum as a fraction. Draw a number line and mark R1, R2, and the answer sitting to the left of both.
dd.analogy: Two doors out of a gym: a wide door and a narrow door. Most students leave through the wide door, so the total exit speed is a bit more than the wide door alone. Doors = resistors (a wide door is a small resistance). It stops working because doors are not about voltage, but the way the easy path wins is the same.
ways: Multiply the two, divide by their sum.
The answer is always a bit smaller than the smaller resistor.

ex.q: A 40 ohm and a 60 ohm resistor are in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
steps: Only two resistors, so product over sum works.
Check: 24 is below 40, the smaller one. Good.

dd.trap: Using product over sum for three or more resistors. It only works for two at a time. Also, do not add the resistors in the bottom only; the bottom is the sum, the top is the product.
dd.tip: Parallel pair: product over sum, the shortcut for just two.

lessons.title: Equal in parallel · A short in parallel

cards.t: Same-size resistors in parallel: divide by how many there are. Three 90 Ω in parallel = 30 Ω.

dd.why: If all n resistors are the same size R, each branch takes the same current. The total current is n times one branch current, with the same voltage. So the total resistance is the voltage divided by n times the branch current, which is R divided by n. Think of it as n identical doors: n times the flow means 1/n of the squeeze. It is a fast shortcut you can check in your head.
dd.pic: Draw three identical boxes in parallel, each labeled 90 ohm. Next to it draw one box labeled 30 ohm. Between them write an equals sign and the words divide by 3.
dd.analogy: Three identical straws in one drink. Drinking through three straws is three times easier than one, so the squeeze is one third. Straws = resistors, ease of drinking = current. It stops working because with straws the sip depends on lungs, but a battery holds a fixed voltage.
ways: n equal resistors in parallel give R divided by n.
Two 100 ohm: 50. Four 100 ohm: 25. Ten 100 ohm: 10.
Plot R/n against n. It curves down quickly: big drop from 1 to 2, smaller drops after.

ex.q: Four 200 ohm resistors are in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
steps: All four are equal, so use R / n.
Check: 50 is less than 200, as parallel should be.
This beats the long reciprocal sum and is easy to do mentally.

dd.trap: Using it when the resistors are different sizes. The shortcut only works for identical resistors. Also do not multiply by n; that would be series.
dd.tip: n twins side by side: divide by n.

cards.t: A 0 Ω path in parallel makes the whole group 0 Ω. All the current takes the short. Dangerous.

dd.why: A short is a path with almost zero resistance. In parallel it gets the same voltage as everything else. By Ohm's law, current is V / R, and with R near zero the current is huge. Nearly all the current takes that easy path, so the other parts get almost nothing and go dark. The huge current heats the wires and the source. That is why shorts cause fires and why fuses exist.
dd.pic: Draw a battery, a lamp, and a plain wire jumping across the lamp from top to bottom. Draw a thick arrow through the wire and a tiny thin arrow through the lamp. Write the lamp voltage as about 0 V.
dd.analogy: A river with a small side channel and a huge waterfall shortcut next to it. Almost all the water takes the shortcut and the mill wheel on the side channel stops. Water = current, mill wheel = the lamp. It stops working because water has no source limit, while a real battery can overheat and be damaged.
ways: A wire across a part gives current a free road. The part gets nothing.
9 V, a 10 ohm resistor, and a 0.1 ohm wire in parallel. Resistor current 0.9 A. Wire current 9 / 0.1 = 90 A. The wire takes 99 percent.
Current always picks the path with the least resistance.

ex.q: A 9 V source has a 10 ohm lamp and a 0.1 ohm wire in parallel. How much current flows in the wire? (Ignore the source resistance.)
steps: Parallel branches all get the full 9 V.
Use I = V / R for the wire branch.
Compare: the lamp only gets 9 / 10 = 0.9 A.
Answer: 90 A in the wire, 100 times more than the lamp.

dd.trap: Students think a short makes the circuit have no current. It does the opposite: a short gives a huge current. The part you shorted goes dark, but the source is in danger.
dd.tip: Short = shortcut, and all the traffic takes it.

cards.t: Shrink the circuit step by step. Combine each parallel group, then each series group, until one resistor is left.

dd.why: A mixed circuit has both series and parallel pieces, so no single rule fits it all. The trick is to shrink it. Find a spot that is clearly parallel or clearly series, replace it with its one equivalent resistor, and redraw. Each step makes the picture simpler without changing what the battery sees. Repeat until one resistor is left. Always work from the inside out, parallel groups first when they sit in a series path.
dd.pic: Draw the original circuit. Circle the parallel group with a pencil. Then draw a second picture with that group replaced by one box. Keep going until you have a single box next to the battery.
dd.analogy: Packing a suitcase inside a bigger suitcase. You pack small bags first, then put those inside bigger ones. Small bags = parallel groups, bigger bag = series path. It stops working because suitcases have size limits, while circuits do not.
ways: Replace each parallel group by one resistor, then add the series parts.
10 ohm in series with two 20 ohm in parallel. 20 || 20 = 10. Then 10 + 10 = 20 ohm.
Parallel first, then series, redraw each time.

ex.q: A 12 ohm resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 30 ohm and 60 ohm. Find the total resistance.
steps: Redraw: the pair becomes one 20 ohm resistor.
Now 12 and 20 are in series, so they add.

dd.trap: Adding everything together without noticing the parallel part. Always ask: is this pair side by side (parallel) or end to end (series)?
dd.tip: Shrink it, redraw it, repeat it.

cards.t: In series, each resistor gets a share of the voltage. Bigger resistor, bigger share.

dd.why: In series, the same current goes through every resistor. Ohm's law then says V = I x R, so a bigger resistor gets a bigger voltage drop. The total drop must equal the battery voltage. So each resistor takes its fraction of the supply, equal to its share of the total resistance. This is the voltage divider. It is how you make a smaller voltage out of a bigger one.
dd.pic: Draw a battery on top, with two stacked resistors in a column and ground at the bottom. Mark the junction in the middle. Write V2 beside the bottom resistor and draw its share as a part of the total height.
dd.analogy: Sharing a pizza by how hungry each person is. A bigger resistor eats a bigger slice of the battery voltage. Pizza = voltage, hunger = resistance. It stops working because pizza slices are food, but voltage does not run out in the wire; it only drops across parts.
ways: Each resistor gets a voltage in proportion to its resistance.
9 V, 2 k and 6 k. Total 8 k. Share of R2 = 6/8. V2 = 6.75 V. V1 = 2.25 V. They add to 9 V.
The bigger resistor gets the bigger share of voltage.

ex.q: A 15 V source feeds R1 = 4 k in series with R2 = 6 k. Find the voltage across R2.
steps: Same current goes through both, so voltage splits by resistance.
Answer: 9 V (and R1 gets 6 V, adding to 15).

dd.trap: Putting the wrong resistor on top. The numerator is the resistor you want the voltage across. Check that the two drops add to the supply.
dd.tip: Big resistor, big slice of the voltage.

cards.t: In parallel, current splits. The smaller resistor takes more.

dd.why: In parallel, both branches have the same voltage, so each current is V / R. The smaller resistor lets more current flow. The total current is the sum of the two. Taking each branch's share gives I1 = I x R2 / (R1 + R2). Notice the other resistor is on top: the branch with less resistance gets the bigger share, so its fraction has the larger number on top.
dd.pic: Draw a wire splitting into two branches. Make the branch with the smaller resistor thicker and the branch with the bigger resistor thinner. Write the currents next to each. Show that they merge again below.
dd.analogy: A crowd leaving a stadium through a wide gate and a narrow gate. More people use the wide gate. Wide gate = small resistance, people = current. It stops working because people choose, while current splits exactly by the math.
ways: Current splits unevenly. The smaller resistor takes the larger share.
12 A into 6 ohm and 3 ohm. R1 gets 12 x 3/9 = 4 A. R2 gets 12 x 6/9 = 8 A. They add to 12 A.
Current goes to the easy path.

ex.q: 20 A splits between R1 = 4 ohm and R2 = 12 ohm in parallel. Find the current in R1.
steps: Both branches share the same voltage, so smaller R gets more current.
Formula: I1 = I x R2 / (R1 + R2).
Check R2: 20 - 15 = 5 A. The 12 ohm gets less, as it should.

dd.trap: Using R1 on top instead of R2, which gives the answer swapped. The smaller resistor must get the bigger current, so check the answer makes sense.
dd.tip: Cross over: the other resistor goes on top.

cards.t: Series bulbs: biggest R is brightest (P = I²R). Parallel bulbs: smallest R is brightest (P = V²/R). Unscrew one parallel bulb and the rest stay lit.

dd.why: Brightness depends on power. In series, current is the same through each bulb, so P = I^2 x R and the bulb with the biggest resistance gets the most power. In parallel, voltage is the same across each bulb, so P = V^2 / R and the bulb with the smallest resistance gets the most power. Each parallel bulb has its own path, so removing one does not stop the others. In series, removing one breaks the only path.
dd.pic: Draw two bulbs in series, then two bulbs in parallel. Under the series picture write I the same and P = I^2 R. Under the parallel picture write V the same and P = V^2 / R. Make the brighter bulb bigger in each picture.
dd.analogy: A relay race versus a group of runners racing side by side. In the relay (series) everyone runs the same number of steps, the one with the heaviest load works hardest. In side by side (parallel) each runner has the same track. Heaviest load = biggest R. It stops working because runners get tired but bulbs do not.
ways: Series: biggest R is brightest. Parallel: smallest R is brightest.
Series, 10 V, bulbs 2 ohm and 8 ohm: I = 1 A, P = 2 W and 8 W. Parallel, 12 V: P = 144/2 = 72 W and 144/8 = 18 W.
Same current: use I^2R. Same voltage: use V^2/R.

ex.q: Bulbs of 2 ohm and 8 ohm are in series across 10 V. Which is brighter, and what is each power?
steps: Current: 10 / 10 = 1 A, the same in both.
Same current, so use P = I^2 x R.
2 ohm bulb: 1 x 1 x 2 = 2 W. 8 ohm bulb: 1 x 1 x 8 = 8 W.
The 8 ohm bulb has more power.
Answer: the 8 ohm bulb is brighter, 8 W versus 2 W.

dd.trap: Using the wrong power formula. In series the current is shared, so use I^2 R. In parallel the voltage is shared, so use V^2 / R. The winner flips.
dd.tip: Series: big R shines. Parallel: small R shines.

cards.t: OPEN: a break, no current, full voltage across the gap. SHORT: tiny resistance, huge current, heat.

dd.why: An open circuit is a break. No charge can cross the gap, so the current is zero everywhere in that series loop. With zero current, the other parts have zero voltage drop (V = I x R = 0), so the whole battery voltage appears across the break. A short is the opposite: a path with tiny resistance. Huge current flows, and that creates heat. Both are faults, but they look very different on a meter.
dd.pic: Draw a loop with a battery, lamp, and a switch. Show the switch open with a gap. Write 0 V across the lamp and 9 V across the gap. Next to it draw the same loop with a thick wire across the lamp and write the words big current.
dd.analogy: A drawbridge. When the bridge is up (open), no cars cross, and all the height difference shows up at the gap. When a tunnel is dug straight through (short), a flood of cars rushes through. Cars = current. It stops working because a bridge gap is not about pressure, but it matches the idea well.
ways: Open: current zero, voltage across the gap is the full battery. Short: current huge, voltage across it near zero.
9 V battery, 100 ohm lamp, switch open: I = 0, lamp 0 V, switch 9 V. Switch closed: I = 0.09 A, lamp 9 V, switch 0 V.
Open = all the voltage. Short = none of the voltage.

ex.q: A 6 V battery, a 50 ohm lamp, and a switch are in series. The switch is open. What is the voltage across the lamp and across the switch?
steps: Open switch means no path, so I = 0.
Lamp: V = I x R = 0 x 50 = 0 V.
The battery voltage must be dropped somewhere.
Kirchhoff: the drops add to 6 V, so the switch has it all.
Check by closing the switch: the lamp would get all 6 V.

dd.trap: Believing that open means 0 V everywhere. The break itself has the full voltage. A meter across an open gap reads the battery voltage.
dd.tip: Open gap, full voltage. Short wire, zero voltage.

cards.t: Voltmeter goes in PARALLEL (high resistance). Ammeter goes in SERIES (tiny resistance). Never put an ammeter across a battery.

dd.why: A voltmeter must not change the circuit it measures, so it has huge resistance and is placed across the part (parallel). Almost no current goes through it. An ammeter must measure the same current that was flowing, so it goes in the path (series) and has tiny resistance. If you put an ammeter across a battery, you make a near short: huge current, a blown fuse, or a damaged meter. If you put a voltmeter in series, its huge resistance blocks nearly all current.
dd.pic: Draw a loop with a battery and a lamp. Draw a circle with V across the lamp (two wires). Draw a second circle with A cut into the loop wire. Label V as parallel and A as series.
dd.analogy: A water meter and a pressure gauge. The flow meter sits in the pipe (series) and counts water passing. The pressure gauge taps the pipe from the side (parallel) and barely uses any water. Flow meter = ammeter, pressure gauge = voltmeter. It stops working because real flow meters slow the water a bit, much as an ammeter adds a tiny resistance.
ways: Voltmeter: parallel, high resistance. Ammeter: series, tiny resistance.
Ammeter 0.1 ohm across 9 V: I = 90 A (bad). Voltmeter 1 Mohm across 9 V: I = 9 microamps (fine).
V is for Voltage, parallel. A is for Amps, series.

ex.q: An ammeter with 0.2 ohm resistance is accidentally connected directly across a 9 V battery. What current would flow (ignore the battery's own resistance)?
steps: The ammeter is in parallel with the battery, a near short.
That is far more than a meter's range or a fuse rating.
Answer: 45 A, which would blow the fuse or damage the meter.

dd.trap: Mixing up where each meter goes. Voltmeters go across a part. Ammeters go in the line with the part. If you need to measure current, break the circuit and insert the meter.
dd.tip: Volts in parallel, amps in series, never amps across a battery.

cards.t: A load gets the most power when its resistance equals the source resistance. Speakers are matched this way.

dd.why: Power in the load is P = I^2 x R. If the load resistance is very small, the current is big but the load voltage is tiny, so power is small. If the load is very big, the voltage is big but the current is tiny, so power is small. Somewhere in the middle there is a peak, and it happens when the load resistance equals the source's own resistance. At that point half the power is lost in the source, so the efficiency is only 50 percent.
dd.pic: Draw a graph with load resistance on the bottom and power up the side. The curve rises quickly, peaks, then falls slowly. Mark the peak where R load = R source.
dd.analogy: Pushing a shopping cart: the best push comes when your effort matches the weight. Too light a load wastes the push and too heavy a load will not move. Effort = source, cart = load. It stops working because the cart does not have a clear peak the way power does.
ways: Maximum power goes to the load when load resistance equals source resistance.
12 V source with 4 ohm inside. Load 2 ohm: 8 W. Load 4 ohm: 9 W. Load 8 ohm: 8 W. The peak is at 4 ohm.
The curve peaks at R load = R source.

ex.q: A 12 V source has 4 ohm of internal resistance. Find the load power for a 4 ohm load.
steps: Load power: P = I^2 x R = 1.5 x 1.5 x 4.
That is the peak: 2 ohm and 8 ohm loads both give 8 W.

dd.trap: Thinking max power also means max efficiency. At the peak, half of the power is wasted inside the source. Also, the card's check question is a simple voltage divider: 12 V across 1 k and 3 k gives 9 V on the 3 k.
dd.tip: Match the load to the source to get the most watts.

cards.t: Power supplied should equal the power used by all resistors. Branch currents should add up. Drops around a loop should add up.

dd.why: Circuits obey conservation laws. Energy cannot appear from nowhere, so the power the source supplies must equal the power the resistors turn into heat. Charge cannot vanish, so currents entering a junction equal currents leaving. Energy per charge cannot go missing around a loop, so the rises and drops balance. If your answers break any of these, you made an arithmetic or setup error. These checks cost seconds and catch most mistakes.
dd.pic: Draw a loop with a battery and three resistors. Write the voltage drop beside each resistor. Under it draw a small bar chart: one tall bar for the battery and three short bars stacked to the same height.
dd.analogy: A bank account: money in must equal money out plus what remains. Battery = deposits, resistors = withdrawals. If the total does not balance, someone made a counting error. It stops working because a bank can run low, while a circuit always balances exactly.
ways: Check power in = power out, branch currents add, loop drops add up.
24 V battery. Drops 5 V and 3 V. Third = 24 - 5 - 3 = 16 V. Sum = 24 V. Balanced.
If it does not add up, something is wrong.

ex.q: A 24 V battery drives three series resistors. Two drop 5 V and 3 V. Find the third drop and check it.
steps: Kirchhoff: drops around the loop add to the battery voltage.
If the current were 2 A, the power would be 48 W from the source and 10 + 6 + 32 = 48 W in the resistors.

dd.trap: Skipping the check. A quick sum catches mistakes like a lost minus sign or a wrong resistor. Add the drops every time.
dd.tip: What goes in must come out: check your sums.

cards.t: SPST: simple on/off. SPDT: switches between two paths. DPST: two on/off switches moved together. DPDT: two SPDT switches moved together.

dd.why: A switch has poles and throws. A pole is one moving contact that carries one circuit. A throw is a position the pole can connect to. The letters in the name count these. Counting terminals is simple: each pole has one common terminal plus one terminal per throw. That is why the four types differ in how many wires they hold and what they can do.
dd.pic: Draw a small box for each type. For SPST draw one lever and one contact. For SPDT draw one lever with two contacts, top and bottom. For DPST draw two SPST levers joined by a dotted line. For DPDT draw two SPDT levers joined by a dotted line.
dd.analogy: A traffic cop at an intersection. One cop (pole) can point cars down one road (SPST) or choose between two roads (SPDT). Two cops moving together are DPST or DPDT. Cop = pole, road = throw. It stops working because cops are not electrically separate, but poles are.
ways: S = single, D = double. P = pole, T = throw. So SPDT is single pole, double throw.
Terminals = poles x (throws + 1). SPST 2. SPDT 3. DPST 4. DPDT 6.
Double pole means two circuits at once. Double throw means two choices.

ex.q: How many terminals does a DPDT switch have, and why?
steps: DPDT means double pole, double throw.
Each pole has one common terminal plus two throw terminals.

dd.trap: Confusing poles with throws. Pole = how many circuits you control. Throw = how many positions each one can connect. Do not just count the letters.
dd.tip: Pole = people, throw = throw-to places.

cards.t: Pole = how many circuits it controls. Throw = how many positions each pole connects to.

dd.why: Pole and throw describe two different jobs. A pole is a circuit the switch controls, so more poles means more circuits switched at once. A throw is a choice of position, so more throws means more places to send current. SPDT sends one circuit to one of two places. Because the name says what it does, you can read it like a label. S or D at the front is the pole count, and S or D at the end is the throw count.
dd.pic: Draw an SPDT switch: a pivot on the left, a lever, and two contacts on the right (top and bottom). Label the pivot as the pole. Label the two contacts as the throws. Draw an arrow showing the lever flipping between them.
