ways: You can only go forward from P or backward from not Q.
P=0, Q=1 makes P -> Q true, Q true, but P false. So Q does not prove P.
Valid: P to Q. Valid: not Q to not P.

ex.q: Given A -> R and A, what follows?
steps: Affirming the first part gives the second.

dd.trap: Thinking Q true proves P. It does not.
dd.tip: Never back from the consequent.

cards.t: Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposites attract. Likes repel. Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets.

dd.why: A magnet's atoms act like tiny magnets lined up the same way. Every one has a north and south end. So if you cut a magnet in half, each half has both poles again. You can never get just one pole. Opposite poles pull together and like poles push apart. That is the same pattern as electric charges, except poles come in pairs.
dd.pic: Draw a bar magnet as a rectangle with N on one end and S on the other. Cut it with a line in the middle and redraw two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S. Draw two magnets with N facing N and arrows pointing apart.
dd.analogy: A pair of shoes: you cannot have a left shoe without a right one. Poles come as a pair. It stops working because shoes can be sold separately, but poles cannot.
ways: Opposites attract, likes repel. No single poles.
Cut one magnet into 3 pieces: you have 3 magnets, 6 poles.

ex.q: A bar magnet is cut into 3 pieces. How many poles are there in all?
steps: Each piece is a full magnet.
Each has one N and one S.

dd.trap: Thinking you can isolate a north pole. They always come in pairs.
dd.tip: Cut it twice, get more twice.

cards.t: They leave north, enter south, and never cross. Closer lines mean a stronger field.

dd.why: Field lines are a map of the magnetic push. They leave the north pole and curve to the south pole outside the magnet. They never cross, because at one point the field can only have one direction. Where lines are packed close, the field is strong, as near the poles. Where lines spread, it is weak.
dd.pic: Draw a bar magnet. Draw curved lines from N around to S, packed tight near the ends and spread out far away. Add small arrowheads along the lines. Draw a compass beside it to show the needle follows a line.
dd.analogy: A weather map with wind arrows: a tight bunch of arrows means strong wind. Lines are arrows, tightness is strength. It stops working because wind is air moving, but a field does not move.
ways: Lines leave N, enter S, never cross, and are dense where the field is strong.
8 lines in a square near the pole versus 2 in a same square far away: 4 times stronger.
Curved loops from N to S.

ex.q: Near a pole 8 field lines pass through a patch. Far away, 2 lines pass through the same size patch. How many times stronger is it near the pole?

dd.trap: Drawing lines that cross. They never do.
dd.tip: Lines leave North, never cross.

cards.t: Iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted (ferromagnetic). Copper, aluminum, and gold are not.

dd.why: Iron, nickel, and cobalt are ferromagnetic. Their atoms group into tiny regions that can line up with an outside magnet. That makes them pulled toward it. Copper, aluminum, and gold do not line up this way, so they are not noticeably attracted. Steel contains iron, so it sticks too. Coins, such as the US penny, are mostly copper.
dd.pic: Draw a bar magnet with three objects near it: an iron nail, a copper wire, and a nickel coin. Draw arrows pulling the nail and nickel in, and an X on the copper.
dd.analogy: Some kids join any club right away (iron), others never join (copper). Magnet is the club invite. It stops working because kids can change their mind, but metals do not.
ways: Iron, nickel, cobalt stick. Copper, aluminum, gold do not.
Fe, Ni, Co: 3 common magnetic metals.

ex.q: Which sticks to a magnet: iron nail, copper wire, aluminum foil, or gold ring?
steps: Look at the metal in each.

dd.trap: Thinking all metals are magnetic. Only a few are.
dd.tip: Fe, Ni, Co: the magnet's pro.

cards.t: A current makes a magnetic field. This was the first link between electricity and magnetism.

dd.why: In 1820 Oersted noticed that a compass needle moved when current flowed in a nearby wire. A compass only reacts to a magnetic field, so the current had to make one. Moving charges create a magnetic field. This was the first proof that electricity and magnetism are linked. Bigger current gives a bigger field, and the field gets weaker with distance.
dd.pic: Draw a wire running up the page with a compass on each side. Draw the compass needles pointing different ways. Add a switch: when off, the needles point north, and when on, they turn.
dd.analogy: A boat's wake: a moving boat disturbs the water around it. The wire's current disturbs space and the compass reacts. Current is the boat, field is the wake. It stops working because a wake dies, but a field stays as long as current flows.
ways: 10 A at 2 cm: about 100 uT. Earth's field is about 50 uT.

ex.q: How strong is the field 2 cm from a wire with 10 A? Use B = 2e-7 x I / r.
steps: Use B = 2 x 10^-7 x I / r.
That is 100 uT, about twice Earth's field.

dd.trap: Thinking only magnets can move a compass. Current can too.
dd.tip: Oersted: wire moves the needle.

cards.t: Straight wire: thumb along the current, fingers curl with the field. Coil: fingers curl with the current, thumb points to north.

dd.why: The field around a wire loops in circles. The right-hand rule tells you the direction. Point your thumb along the conventional current. Your curled fingers show how the field circles. For a coil, flip the idea: curl your fingers the way the current goes around, and your thumb points to the north end. This works every time, so you do not have to memorize pictures.
dd.pic: Draw a wire as a dot for current coming out of the page. Draw a circle around it with arrows going counterclockwise. Then draw a wire as an X for current into the page with arrows clockwise.
dd.analogy: A screw: turning a screw clockwise drives it away from you. Current is the screw's travel, field is the turn. It stops working because a screw has threads and wires do not.
ways: Thumb along current, fingers show the field circles.
5 A at 5 cm: B = 20 uT, counterclockwise if current points out of the page.

ex.q: Current flows out of the page in a straight wire. Which way does the field circle, and how strong at 5 cm with 5 A?
steps: Point the right thumb out of the page.

dd.trap: Using the left hand, or using electron flow. Use the right hand and conventional current.
dd.tip: Right thumb, current's way.

cards.t: More turns, more current, and an iron core all make it stronger. It turns off when the current stops.

dd.why: A coil of wire adds the field of every turn, so more turns make a stronger field. More current makes a stronger field too. A soft iron core inside gets magnetized by the coil, and adds its own field, often hundreds of times more. When the current stops, the core loses its magnetism, so the magnet turns off. That makes electromagnets useful in cranes and relays.
dd.pic: Draw a nail wrapped with 8 turns of wire, with wires to a battery. Draw field lines out of one end and back into the other. Mark N on the end where your thumb points using the coil rule.
dd.analogy: A crowd cheering: each person adds noise (turns), louder voices (current), and a megaphone (core) multiplies it. It stops working because a crowd noise never has a clean off switch.
ways: More turns, more current, iron core.
500 turns over 0.1 m with 0.2 A in air: about 1.3 mT.
Double the turns, double the field.

ex.q: A coil has 500 turns over 0.1 m and carries 0.2 A. Find B in air, B = 4 pi e-7 x (N/L) x I.
steps: B is about 1.3 mT in air, and an iron core would raise it much more.

dd.trap: Thinking a bigger battery is the only way. Turns and the core matter too.
dd.tip: Turns, amps, iron: three ways to strengthen.

cards.t: A motor turns electricity into motion. A generator turns motion into electricity. Moving a magnet through a coil makes voltage.

dd.why: A moving magnet near a coil changes the magnetic field through the coil. A changing field pushes charges and makes a voltage. This is induction. Faster motion, a stronger magnet, or more turns makes more voltage. A generator turns a coil in a field to make this on purpose. A motor is the reverse: current in a field makes a force that turns.
dd.pic: Draw a coil connected to a meter. Draw a bar magnet moving into the coil with an arrow. Show the needle jumping while the magnet moves and staying at zero when it stops.
dd.analogy: A paddle wheel in a river: the faster the water moves, the more power it makes. Magnet speed is water speed. It stops working because a still magnet in a coil does nothing, but a still river wheel can still hold water.
ways: Changing field through a coil makes voltage.
100 turns, flux change 0.002 Wb in 0.1 s: 2 V. With 200 turns: 4 V.

ex.q: A 100-turn coil sees a flux change of 0.002 Wb in 0.1 s. What voltage? What if turns double?
steps: Use V = N x change in flux / time.

dd.trap: Thinking a still magnet in a coil makes voltage. It must move or change.
dd.tip: Move the magnet, make the volts.

cards.t: Needs AC. More turns on the secondary means higher voltage.

dd.why: A transformer has two coils on a shared iron core. AC in the primary makes a changing field. That field goes through the secondary and induces a voltage. Each turn gets the same voltage, so the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio. More secondary turns give a higher voltage, and fewer give a lower one. It needs AC, since DC makes a steady field that induces nothing. An ideal transformer keeps power the same, so current changes the other way.
dd.pic: Draw an iron ring. Wrap 200 turns on the left and 50 turns on the right. Write 120 V AC on the left and a question mark on the right. Draw arrows for the field going around the ring.
dd.analogy: Gears: a big gear turning a small gear makes it spin faster. Turns are gear teeth. It stops working because gears trade speed for force, while transformers trade volts for amps.

ex.q: Ideal transformer: Np = 200, Ns = 50, primary 120 V AC. Find Vs.

dd.trap: Feeding it DC. Without change there is no induced voltage.
dd.tip: Turns up, volts up.

cards.t: Two metal plates with an insulator between. It stores energy in an electric field.

dd.why: When a battery connects to the plates, it pushes electrons onto one plate and pulls them off the other. The plates now hold opposite charges. They attract each other across the gap, but the insulator will not let electrons cross. So the charges just sit there, pulling on each other. That pull is an electric field in the gap, and the field holds the stored energy. If the gap were a conductor, the charge would flow across and nothing would be stored.
dd.pic: Draw two parallel horizontal lines for the plates. Put plus signs along the top one and minus signs along the bottom one. Draw short arrows in the gap pointing from the top plate down to the bottom plate. Those arrows are the field.
dd.analogy: Think of a stretched rubber band held between two fingers. The stretch is the stored energy. The plates are your fingers, the charge difference is the stretch, and the field is the tension. It breaks down because a rubber band stretches for any size, but a real capacitor has a voltage limit where the insulator fails.
ways: Charge separated by an insulator stores energy in the gap, not in the metal.
Connect a 9 V battery, then remove it. The plates keep their opposite charge and still show 9 V on a meter.
Capacitor = tiny short-term energy tank. A battery = big long-term energy tank.

ex.q: A 100 uF capacitor is charged to 9 V. How much energy is in its field?
steps: Use the energy formula E = 1/2 C V^2 because the energy is in the field.

dd.trap: Thinking the energy sits inside the metal plates. It sits in the electric field in the insulating gap.
dd.tip: Plates plus a gap: charge can't hop, so it waits and pulls.

cards.t: How much charge it holds per volt. Unit: farad (F). Most are µF.

dd.why: Capacitance tells how easily a capacitor takes in charge for each volt pushed on it. Bigger plates have more room for charge. Plates closer together pull harder on each other, so more charge fits at the same voltage. The ratio Q/V stays the same for a given capacitor, so it is a fixed property, like the size of a bucket. A farad is huge, which is why real parts use microfarads (uF).
dd.pic: Draw a bucket. The width of the bucket is the capacitance C. The water level is the voltage V. The amount of water is the charge Q. Mark the level with a line and shade the water below it.
dd.analogy: A wide bucket versus a narrow bucket: at the same water level, the wide one holds more water. Bucket width is C, water level is V, water volume is Q. It stops working because a bucket can be any shape, while capacitance is fixed by plate area and gap only.
ways: Capacitance is charge stored per volt.
C = 10 uF. At 2 V: Q = 20 uC. At 4 V: Q = 40 uC. Q doubles when V doubles.
Plot Q (up) against V (across). It is a straight line through zero. The slope is C.

ex.q: A capacitor holds 30 uC of charge at 6 V. What is C?
steps: Pick the formula C = Q / V.
Write Q = 30 uC and V = 6 V.
Units: uC per volt is uF.

dd.trap: Mixing units. uF and uC are millionths. Keep the prefix on both and the answer stays clean.
dd.tip: Farad = bucket size. Charge per volt.

cards.t: Double the voltage and the energy is 4 times bigger.

lab.hook: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field.

dd.why: The voltage squared appears because there are two things growing at once. To add more charge you must push against the charge already there. Double the voltage means double the charge on the plates, and each bit of charge is pushed in at double the voltage. Two doubles make a quadruple. So energy rises with the square of V. That is why a small voltage rise can make a capacitor much more dangerous.
dd.pic: Draw a graph of V (up) against Q (across). It is a straight line from the origin. Shade the triangle under the line. The area of that triangle, 1/2 x Q x V, is the stored energy.
dd.analogy: Compressing a spring: the more it is squeezed, the harder you must push, so the second half costs more than the first. Squeeze is the charge, push is the voltage. It stops working because a spring has a break point set by metal, but a capacitor limit is set by the insulator.
ways: Half the voltage gives one fourth of the energy.
C = 10 uF. 5 V gives 125 uJ. 10 V gives 500 uJ. Twice the volts, four times the energy.
Change V by a factor of k and energy changes by k^2.

ex.q: Voltage across a 20 uF capacitor goes from 5 V to 15 V. How many times bigger is the energy?
steps: Energy depends on V^2, so compare squares.
At 15 V E = 2250 uJ, which is 9 times 250 uJ.

dd.trap: Saying double voltage gives double energy. Square it: double gives four times.
dd.tip: Volts squared, joules shared.

cards.t: Parallel: capacitances add. Series: use the reciprocal rule (opposite of resistors).

dd.why: Parallel capacitors act like one bigger set of plates, so their areas add and capacitance adds. In series, the charge on each one must be the same, and the voltage splits between them. The total gap the voltage must cross is longer, so less charge fits per volt. That is why series gives a smaller total, the opposite of resistors. Series total is always less than the smallest one.
dd.pic: Draw two capacitors side by side between the same two wires for parallel. Then draw them end to end on one wire for series. Label parallel Plates add. Label series Gaps add.
dd.analogy: Parallel is like two buckets filling from the same tap: the total space adds. Series is like a bucket with a second bucket stacked below it, sharing the same stream. It stops working because the series stack is about voltage sharing, which water does not show well.
ways: Parallel: add. Series: reciprocal rule, like parallel resistors.
4 uF and 12 uF. Parallel: 16 uF. Series: (4 x 12)/(4 + 12) = 3 uF.
Capacitors do the opposite of resistors. Parallel adds, series shrinks.

ex.q: Find the series capacitance of 6 uF and 3 uF.
steps: Two capacitors, so product over sum works.
18 / 9 = 2 uF, smaller than 3 uF, which makes sense.

dd.trap: Using the resistor rules by habit. Capacitors flip them: parallel adds.
dd.tip: Caps are the mirror of resistors.

cards.t: Once fully charged, it blocks steady current like an open circuit.

dd.why: A capacitor charges until its voltage equals the supply. Once they match, nothing pushes more charge on. The current drops to zero. The insulator in the gap blocks any steady flow, so for steady DC it looks like a broken wire. During charging, current flows briefly. After that, it is quiet. If the capacitor still passed steady current, the plates could not hold a charge.
dd.pic: Draw a circuit with a battery, a resistor, and a capacitor in a loop. Draw an arrow on the wire labeled big at the start. Then draw the same arrow crossed out later with the label zero.
dd.analogy: A balloon being blown up through a pipe: at first air rushes in, then the balloon is full and the air stops. Air flow is current, balloon pressure is capacitor voltage. It stops working because a balloon can pop slowly and leak, while a good capacitor holds its charge.
ways: Full capacitor: no more current, so treat it as open.
9 V battery, 1 kilohm resistor, capacitor. Start: 9 mA. Later: 0 mA, and the capacitor reads 9 V.
Plot current against time: it starts high and falls to zero. Plot capacitor voltage: it starts at zero and rises to 9 V.

ex.q: A 12 V battery, a 2 kilohm resistor, and a capacitor are in series. After a long time, what is the current and the capacitor voltage?
steps: A full capacitor blocks steady current, so I = 0.
With I = 0, the resistor drops V = I x R = 0.
All 12 V must be across the capacitor.

dd.trap: Saying the capacitor has no voltage when current stops. Zero current means full voltage.
dd.tip: Full cap, closed gap? No: full cap, open gap.
